Subject: SGE Internship Application Follow Up
Body:
Hi Graham,

 

Thank you for your interest in Susquehanna Growth Equity (SGE)! To begin your interview process for our open positions, you will need to complete a brief recorded video submission. You will receive a separate email from admin.mettl@mercer.com <mailto:admin.mettl@mercer.com> , our third-party administrator, with a link to complete your submission.

 

We share this with candidates to provide an opportunity to elaborate on their interest in the industry and SGE, beyond what is outlined on your resume. We value responses that are logical, well-structured, concise, and coherent. There is no right or wrong answer.

 

When you open the video link, there will be instructions about submitting your video. Once you click start, a 20-minute timer will begin. There will be two prompts that you will be required to record and submit video responses to. Your response time will be limited to 2-minutes for each prompt. You will not be able to pause the timer once it begins, and you will not be able to rerecord your responses.

 

Once the 20-minute timer begins, we recommend that you take approximately 8 minutes to review the first question and outline your response, and then record your response. Once you have completed your response to the first question, you should click “Next Section” to review the second prompt and repeat that process.  

 

Please note that you will be responsible for monitoring your own time as you will not be given any warnings before the overall 20-minute timer expires, or before the 2-minute time limit for each response expires. We also encourage having a pen and paper with you so that you can outline your ideas before recording your video responses.

 

If you open any other windows or navigate away from the browser for any reason, you will be kicked out of the video submission link and will be unable to resubmit your video. This includes any automatic pop-ups, so please make sure these features are disabled before you begin this exercise.

 

As we noted above, this assessment is administered by Mettl. By applying for this job, you gave Susquehanna your consent to share your email address with Mettl solely for purposes of administering the assessment. If you wish to review how we handle and protect your personal data, please review our Privacy Statement <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftracking.icims.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FUq99P-int7TcLgFnNx8qJg~~%2FAAIB5hA~%2Fs0_B92JCS_rT5qzMSQLYjAuhI8SNE2f4dW9yD35Oq_FotH2crDonZaiisszqIsXR2w12ZaEszk4wSnZ1NE5V1u4I8RiRMt23NblO-pGKJq1YIeQROW1fddENbLlXWwAZ&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C1403301ee8424c524d6208de998d44f1%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639117029198655224%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=DHdXkeRrmvQjFWi8kHUsTVDmQ0SMyJxHi3KB0Aoy49Y%3D&reserved=0> .

Join DuQIS and SSMU for a seminar featuring Henry Pfister, Addy Family Professor of ECE and Math at Duke! Prof. Pfister's research spans classical and quantum information theory, error correction, communications, and machine learning. He will discuss some of his recent work.

Hi team!  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/smile.png?v=15> 

We want to share with you the critically important that we received for the 260210-perception-video-shot-correction project (the client sent this feedback today).

It’s really important that you review this content carefully and apply it to your next tasks  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/down_arrow.png?v=15> 

*	Missing segment cuts: clearly new events / actions are being missed, camera cuts, perspective changes, etc.
*	Cuts slightly mis-timed: cuts are starting either too early or too late- not on exact frames as we have stressed the importance of.
*	Needing more granular segmentation: many long shots should be split into their distinct actions / events.
*	Incorrect / unhelpful scene labeling: labels should describe what’s happening, rather than generic labels like “scene” or describing the camera movement (should be describing what’s actually happening in the scene).

Thank you for your hard work!  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/raising_hands.png?v=15>

Our annual symposium is a celebration of ongoing research from across campus being conducted by our talented undergraduate students.

This year, the Duke Undergraduate Research Symposium will feature student research flash talks in addition to poster presentations. Students who feel as though their research is best shared in a talk format will get the chance to share alongside peers who choose to present a poster.

Also new this year, our symposium will have a session featuring Distinguished Senior Thesis Talks. Seniors pursuing Graduation with Distinction are invited to apply to give one of these talks. Three senior students, one each from Natural & Quantitative Sciences, Social Sciences, and Arts & Humanities, will be selected to present on their senior thesis research.

Duke Community: We invite you to attend our annual symposium to show your support of our undergraduate researchers and get a sense of the vast research being done in Arts & Humanities, Social Sciences, and Natural & Quantitative Sciences here on our campus.

This event is produced in partnership with Muser and Duke University Libraries.

In this workshop, participants will explore the beauty of the plants, bugs, and surroundings of the Duke Gardens, and learn to document their observations in words and sketches. Whether you are a budding bird or bug watcher, seasoned nature lover, or have never given a thought to keeping a nature journal, The Art of Noticing workshop will help you hone skills to become a careful observer to the natural world. Workshop leaders will guide you through a hands on experience in both plein air sketching and nature journaling, and hopefully set you off on a journey to a new way of noticing the world around you beyond Duke Gardens. All attendees will receive a field note book to use and take home.

*This is a community workshop open to all.

Hi students! Please see below for this week’s DFE Student News and Events newsletter.

 

DFE News & Events:

AmplifyME Finance Simulations – available through the summer!

Explore roles in banking, markets, and Quant while building real-world skills, tracking performance, and accessing potential recruiting opportunities with top firms. AmplifyME’s live, virtual simulations are open to all Duke undergraduates and will be available through August 31. Learn more at econ.duke.edu/dfe/finance-simulations-amplifyme <https://econ.duke.edu/dfe/finance-simulations-amplifyme> .

Create an account <https://pathways.amplifyme.com/uni/signup/S58GKIE>  on the AmplifyME platform with verification code 779495 and your Duke email address (see onboarding instructions <https://econ.duke.edu/sites/econ.duke.edu/files/documents/Pathways%20Onboarding%20Instructions%20PDF_0.pdf> ).  View the schedule of upcoming simulations. <https://hs-6845477.f.hubspotemail.net/hubfs/6845477/Pathways%20Weekly%20Finance%20Simulations%20-%20w_c%2013th%20April.pptx.pdf?utm_medium=email&_hsenc=p2ANqtz-_eDf2AhRqpYTgmTNVWkRmqpApL49nVeCr51vzaJm4dJ6ddO-HOn1_cdtpQjQmCR2QHlgvqsFy9OhpQTLpQMTJqCy9qZ5b-l2QJOq3H2FF4yKHKci0&_hsmi=412978085&utm_content=412978085&utm_source=hs_email> 

 

DFE Advising Opportunities:

DFE Peer-to-Peer Advising for Sophomores – FINAL WEEK of ADVISING SESSIONS!

As a resource for your finance recruitment-related questions, five upperclassmen are offering drop-in office hours weekly on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday in Soc Sci 228A. For the student advisors’ schedules and bios, go to econ.duke.edu/dfe/eichel-finance-advising-network <https://econ.duke.edu/dfe/eichel-finance-advising-network>  under the Other Advising Opportunities heading.

Alumni Advising with Mark Augusti – open to all undergraduates  REGISTER <https://www.signupgenius.com/go/10C0F44ABAE29A7F5CF8-59754216-finance> 

Mondays through April 20th , 12:00 – 1:00 PM, in the DFE Conference Room (Social Sciences 228A) 

Mark Augusti ‘87 holds weekly in-person advising hours for undergrads. This spring, Augusti teaches FMKT 390S-04: Financing Health Care Companies. Read his bio below:

Mark Augusti, MBA, is Founder and Managing Owner of Kenmore Advisors, an advisory and consulting firm focused on compliance, governance, and commercial strategy in the medical technology sector. Previously, Mr. Augusti was President and Chief Executive Officer and a member of the Board of Directors at Conformis, Inc., a public orthopedic device company. Prior to leading Conformis, Mr. Augusti was Integra LifeSciences Corporation’s Corporate Vice President and President of Orthopedics and Tissue Technologies. Mr. Augusti served as Chief Executive Officer at Bioventus LLC, and was a member of the Bioventus’ Board of Directors. Prior to that Mr. Augusti spent nine years with Smith & Nephew, in a series of leadership roles within the orthopedics and biologics businesses. Prior to that, he spent 13 years at GE Medical Systems, where he held various sales, marketing and strategic management roles, both in the U.S. and internationally. Mr. Augusti serves as a director of the Massachusetts Health Policy Forum and has served as a director of the AdvaMed Accel Board. Mr. Augusti received his M.B.A. from the UCLA Anderson School of Management, and his B.S. in Computer Science and Economics from Duke University.

Career Everywhere Drop-In Advising – open to undergraduates and graduate students
Tuesday, April 21, 1:00-3:00 PM in the DFE Conference Room (Social Sciences 228A)

Meet with Duke Career Center for 15-minute Drop-In Advising for quick questions, document reviews, etc. Time slots will be on a first-come, first-served on-site basis, the day of the event. NO REGISTRATION REQUIRED. Available to all undergraduate students and graduate students from the Duke Graduate School, Duke’s Pratt School of Engineering (PhD only), Duke Divinity School, Duke Medicine School’s Master of Biostatistics and Population Health Sciences programs. Market Recap 	
Week of Apr. 6 through Apr. 10, 2026 	
The S&P 500 <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrack.pstmrk.it%2F3s%2Fycharts.com%252Findices%252F%25255ESPX%2FOaA%2FJ6PHAQ%2FAQ%2F2b140d9d-3a25-4e3b-a939-dcd389fa4234%2F3%2FtpyDYE1UIz&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C672f463f9a2548954efd08de99603cad%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116835837045162%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=btVItOpNX86%2FoAEvUFumIXvCKTEXzIZO%2Ff4zfY5MfMw%3D&reserved=0>  index rose 3.6% this week in a broad climb ahead of high-stakes peace talks between Iran and the US and the Q1 earnings reporting season.

The S&P 500 ended the week at 6,816.89, its second positive week in a row. The index is up 4.4% for April, erasing much of March's 4.6% drop. It is down 0.4% for the year.

A two-week ceasefire reached between the US and Iran early this week appeared to be holding as officials from Washington and Tehran were expected to meet on Saturday in Pakistan, which helped broker the ceasefire.

The coming week also marks the unofficial start of the Q1 earnings reporting season.

US consumer sentiment hit the lowest on record this month, reflecting heightened worries about higher prices and the overall economic fallout from the Middle East conflict, according to the University of Michigan's preliminary April survey. The survey was largely completed before the announcement of the two-week ceasefire.

A report by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed US consumer inflation accelerated to its highest monthly reading in nearly four years in March as the Middle East conflict sent energy prices sharply higher. The data showed energy price growth jumped about 11% sequentially in March, led by a 21% surge in gasoline, accounting for nearly three quarters of the headline increase.

Every sector other than energy rose this week. Communication services and consumer discretionary climbed 5.8% each, followed by a 4.8% gain in technology and a 4.7% advance in industrials. Materials were also strong, up 3.5%, while real estate and financials rose more than 2% each. Utilities, consumer staples and health care also edged higher.

Amazon.com (AMZN) <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrack.pstmrk.it%2F3s%2Fycharts.com%252Fcompanies%252FAMZN%2FOaA%2FJ6PHAQ%2FAQ%2F2b140d9d-3a25-4e3b-a939-dcd389fa4234%2F4%2Fauc5FvmKOC&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C672f463f9a2548954efd08de99603cad%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116835837068981%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=4cwJbZeFRlrzZUW%2FmYJyGE8LfvMPH7O8Xbixtf9AZ0U%3D&reserved=0>  was the top performer in consumer discretionary, climbing 14%. Spring is in full swing and we have just the events to celebrate!

On Tuesday, visit the Spring Craft Fair, the final event hosted by DUU’s first-year interns, then check out Duke@Nite’s No Sleep ’Till Finals event, where you can pick up goodies and cookies to make finals season a little sweeter. On Wednesday, don’t miss the return of the ferris wheel on Abele at Spring on the Quad, birdhouse painting with VisArts, or a night of Grateful Dead covers at Coffeehouse. Wrap up the week with one (or more!) of four movie screenings, and as always, enjoy even more events happening all week long.

hemlock is the swamp-raised, “phone-fi" alt-folk project of multi-disciplinary creative force Carolina Chauffe, currently anchored between Louisiana and Chicago, but more often on the highway.

Doggedly DIY, they have toured nearly nonstop for the past few years on “permatour”, prioritizing non-traditional and alternative venue spaces such as house shows. Both following and expanding true folk tradition, they strive to return music to where it has always existed - the porch, the waterside, the field, the home.

Iceblink is a homespun, intimate project conjured by Lynn Avery in Minneapolis. As a trans woman, everything she creates is about her experience and Lynn describes "Carpet Cocoon" as her comfort album, music to retreat to in the winter. Informed by her passion for mixtapes, oddities and crate digging blogs, the album is eclectic yet cohesively spun around the aesthetic of a bedroom new age album. Sonically, it has a fuzzy and rounded vibe incorporating nylon string guitars through vocoders, textural Prophet synthesizers, flutes and filtered saxophone. The effect of "Carpet Cocoon" is stunning and personal, melancholic yet idyllic, a spiritual ritual of baths for lying on your bedroom floor.

Session 1: Private Company Valuation 

Tuesday, April 14th, 2026 | 10:00 – 11:30 am EDT 


Join us to explore the methodologies and complexities involved in valuing private companies, including key analytical challenges, financial statement nuances, and valuation techniques specific to private firms. Participants will examine the adjustments required to move from reported financials to an enterprise value framework suitable for investment and transaction analysis. 
________________________________

Session 2: Private Company Operating Model 

Wednesday, April 15th, 2026 | 10:00 – 11:30 am EDT 


This session centers on building a detailed operating model for a private company using information from a Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM). Emphasis is placed on preparing supporting financial schedules and translating business assumptions into a coherent forecast that serves as the foundation for valuation and deal analysis. 
________________________________

Session 3: Private Company LBO 

Thursday, April 16th, 2026 | 10:00 – 11:30 am EDT 


This session applies the completed operating model to valuation and leveraged buyout (LBO) analysis, linking forecasts to capital structure, returns, and transaction outcomes. Participants review how operating assumptions, valuation approach, and deal structure interact and are ultimately justified in an investment context.

On Their Tippy Toes

 

Baseball players don’t get to calculate their own batting averages, but they’ve had lots of leeway about one stat that mattered to them—how tall they are.

 

With this year’s adoption of Automated Ball-Strike technology, Major League Baseball made everyone undergo strict height measurements. Much like online dating profiles, it turns out that athletes like saying they’re at least 6 feet tall if they can do it with a straight face. The Athletic reports <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45173149.473343%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubnl0aW1lcy5jb20vYXRobGV0aWMvNzE1NTYyNi8yMDI2LzAzLzMwL21sYi1zaG9ydC1raW5ncy1oZWlnaHQtbWVhc3VyZW1lbnRzLWNoYW5naW5nLWFicy8_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB953e0de7&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C1f542cf44ca2427d0b6008de994a02ed%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116740337243540%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Ay%2Ft9x8i%2FVoLlcBNYBHBqpL4cT32l3AY8B87erG6f2U%3D&reserved=0>  that the opening day roster lost a collective 20 feet of height with a cluster winding up at 5 feet 10 or 11 inches.

 

If only mutual funds were held to such strict measurements. You’ve probably heard, for example, that a majority of active managers fail to beat their benchmark in the long run. But, like a batter doubling as umpire, the rules allow funds to tweak their strike zone after the fact in fund literature.

 

Professors Kevin Mullally and Andrea Rossi found that <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45173149.473343%2FaHR0cHM6Ly9wYXBlcnMuc3Nybi5jb20vc29sMy9wYXBlcnMuY2ZtP2Fic3RyYWN0X2lkPTQxNDU4ODMmbW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB82b4600d&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C1f542cf44ca2427d0b6008de994a02ed%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116740337268402%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Es%2BEZ7vjWSvDndEtvT1lDFGCa0WxeVt49Fm3EKc2lnA%3D&reserved=0>  more than a third of funds they sampled over a 12-year stretch changed their benchmark at least once. It was generally in a way that flattered their returns. That might mean swapping the S&P 500 for the Russell 1000 or moving to an index that emphasizes value or growth instead.

 

The technique was most common among high-fee funds or those sold by brokers, and it had a positive effect on inflows. But it gets worse: Financial firms raise their entire industry’s stat line by showing only those funds they kept open.

 

Dimensional Fund Advisors, which advocates passive investing, studied actively managed stock mutual funds <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45173149.473343%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZGltZW5zaW9uYWwuY29tL3VzLWVuL2luc2lnaHRzL3doeS13b3JyeS1hYm91dC1zdXJ2aXZvcnNoaXAtYmlhcz9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB4ba03923&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C1f542cf44ca2427d0b6008de994a02ed%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116740337310311%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ry%2B%2FNUDqC%2BTSMnhDDwv1aHXAjsZk4caC3Nzr%2BUUD4ao%3D&reserved=0>  between 1991 and 2020. Over that time an average of about 100 funds were liquidated each year, with 2009, the trough of a bear market, seeing the highest number.

 

Poorly performing funds are most likely to get the chop. The median surviving fund still trailed what its return should have been by 0.84 percentage points a year. That would have been a much worse 1.44 percentage point gap if defunct funds had been counted.

 

Finally, there are Morningstar’s influential ratings. A 2024 study <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45173149.473343%2FaHR0cHM6Ly9wYXBlcnMuc3Nybi5jb20vc29sMy9wYXBlcnMuY2ZtP2Fic3RyYWN0X2lkPTQ5NzEyMjgmbW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dCcb3bbce8&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C1f542cf44ca2427d0b6008de994a02ed%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116740337334430%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=DSM7J2GwGPbpjO%2BJqajCCm%2Bh%2Bd1tZRQXqi2IyRTK7Is%3D&reserved=0>  says some funds intentionally change their holdings to land in a weaker category where they’re likely to earn more stars—a technique called “box jumping.” It’s akin to a team switching to a weaker division midseason to earn a playoff spot based on the same record.

 

Not that stars tell us much: A Journal study <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45173149.473343%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9hcnRpY2xlcy90aGUtbW9ybmluZ3N0YXItbWlyYWdlLTE1MDg5NDY2ODc_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBce75912c&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C1f542cf44ca2427d0b6008de994a02ed%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116740337358240%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=GP%2BuXfOVHNQq0R1UGOsQ8bRxBK490gxWuOj%2FrtcUSTk%3D&reserved=0>  in 2017 showed that five-star funds often regress to being just average after winning the accolade. About 10% fall to the lowly one-star category.

 

Talk about a nasty slider.

✏️ MAGA’s top antitrust fixer pushes U.S. officials to approve his deals with threats and insults. A WSJ investigation found that Mike Davis has pressured antitrust officials at the Justice Department <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-ghhihkd-hrkusddg-h%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ce03692661afc4ec8a50c08de873bf2c5%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096888744288840%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Lb6fRjSvdQhyXOjVAEZdpSbLUlRy26n6nJE2PZUbueY%3D&reserved=0>  to approve his deals—and gone over their heads when they didn’t. His approach underscores a new reality at the DOJ that’s worrying even some of President Trump’s loyalists: Some mergers now get approval or draw mild settlements based on political ties rather than public interest, according to current and former antitrust officials. 

Emma Tucker
Editor in Chief, The Wall Street Journal


TODAY'S HEADLINES

1

*	Iran believes it’s winning the war <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-ghhihkd-hrkusddg-k%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ce03692661afc4ec8a50c08de873bf2c5%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096888744312187%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7thTudHBekiU8CR9cTfd7Dl6AAetVxVxuXUAuKf75EM%3D&reserved=0>  and can impose a settlement on Washington that entrenches its control of Middle East energy supplies, writes Yaroslav Trofimov.
*	Trump said the U.S. is considering “winding down” its operation against Iran after earlier saying he was not open to a cease-fire. Follow live updates here <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-ghhihkd-hrkusddg-u%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ce03692661afc4ec8a50c08de873bf2c5%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096888744343715%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=BMlLr4sj1MyeE6TCDm8Ng1n0qiVai8%2BewdUr%2FXou2s0%3D&reserved=0> .
*	Meanwhile, the U.S. is racing to ship air defenses and counter-drone systems <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-ghhihkd-hrkusddg-o%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ce03692661afc4ec8a50c08de873bf2c5%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096888744359468%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=LmjV08SmUufJ6srp6r2z%2Fbp2gkK7od3xrBPrByfNMh8%3D&reserved=0>  to the region, and the war is putting U.S. embassies in the crosshairs <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-ghhihkd-hrkusddg-b%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ce03692661afc4ec8a50c08de873bf2c5%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096888744385336%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=ifHHUnS91HXWkaX0ChMqKt6ukdFgGkAdtOQk48MlHKk%3D&reserved=0> .

FROM THE MARKETS

Q: Reaching America’s middle class is difficult. How are people pulling it off? 


Rising up from poverty isn’t easy. Reporters Te-Ping Chen and Lauren Weber wrote about the paths Americans are taking <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-ghhihkd-hrkusddg-w%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ce03692661afc4ec8a50c08de873bf2c5%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096888744582640%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=rjEMBbuipWhkd4n23hLKauHg%2FfaeQefw5WaSKv0JyXE%3D&reserved=0>  to do it.

A: The ability to climb the economic ladder has been a hallmark of the American experience. Yet children born to low-earning parents in 1992 had a harder time moving into the middle class than the previous generation, according to Opportunity Insights. Today’s paths to the middle class don’t just run through college or traditional manufacturing work. The Americans who make it are open to change, are persistent and jump at unconventional opportunities.

For example, LeAngela Runels, 29, grew up poor in the Detroit area. In high school, Runels was sometimes homeless and stayed with friends. To pay the bills at Eastern Michigan University, she worked two jobs. In 2017, she dropped out in her junior year after a surprise pregnancy. She started a cleaning business during the pandemic, toddler in tow, but made only around $1,000 a month.

Then, in 2022, a cleaning client who was an executive at a local Goodwill told her about its job programs. One involved making outdoor furniture from wooden pallets. Her instructors there referred her to another program: welding. Runels now makes $21 an hour welding for a metal-recycling company, and combined with her cleaning company, earns around $55,000 a year. She hopes to eventually start her own company repairing trailers and railings.

Today is the first full day of spring. Can you feel it? In the Northeast, it was mostly cold and rainy this week, and one could only repeat “In like a lion, out like a lamb” and check the weather apps again. We’re technically in Spring of Deception, according to a meme that posits 12 actual seasons <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fa%2FdOUmSyBzFF0Yt6_LAacwvA~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FLjdPbvqCgjkkoFHDaymYzJFDkzEgEGZ2WmG3uJkwCMSAvVC1p3pzmsGLFatWJd8laI5ilfYACvzQgWTUUA0dZbSLehH_YxxoyVuZofE_16mEMGkEVwxs5Eksu1UYAcndBDmXjPz1YtY3G9ibI2ZGYESMoESRqWCeuhkstwKVJ_3G9_eGs0vGTxCOvKkwGmbRZhxeO7xTyD0sNlbUNEsDOuCqqw4Y2cIhAOYwjD_FLAUAYk54px9KQvTt1R4QYLPBLIl9-iuB-xdEyYIUEztbO4v_BFagVVPvSElmdR_bOCg~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C5b1e6071799b489c1f6f08de8730e77c%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096841303043826%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=W2asNBTCc2gjnZqL3EnDSMa4l%2BOYsJn2dtK0I0JMVUc%3D&reserved=0> , based on experience rather than science. (Next up is Third Winter, followed by The Pollening.)

Even so, once the equinox passes, the good weather bias begins. We increasingly expect warmer days, note the early perennials sending up their shoots in flower beds still pocked with snow. We underdress optimistically when the temperature grazes heights not seen since fall.

I’m too eager, a spring-summer dogmatist wishing it Memorial Day so fervently I overlook the grass greening. I miss commuters’ coffee cups transitioning from hot to iced, the gradual unbuttoning and disappearance of coats. My friend Austin remarked that the seasons are one of the few things left we can’t change on demand — they take as long as they take and there’s no app or hack to speed their progress. He meant this as a good thing.

And he’s right, of course. These early technically spring days, with their absurd cold gusts and flashes of pale sun, are still days. They still contain 24 hours to inhabit, even if I wish I were inhabiting them in shorts. Anticipation is tricky: It feels exciting to look forward to something, but often that looking forward results in overlooking what’s right here. Right here, just on the other side of the equinox, daylight now exceeds dark in the Northern Hemisphere. Each day, sunset is a little bit later.

“What is all this juice and all this joy?” Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote in his poem “Spring.” Indeed, what is it? What’s with the dampness of sidewalks, the smell of the thawing earth? Are there more birds singing or am I just waking up to them? They’re the tiny increments of spring arriving. The equinox is a planetary demarcation, but real-life spring arrives gradually, a halting, nonlinear progression. Residue of winter, hints of future summer, doubling back before settling into itself, a season getting its footing, finally, eventually, again.

	
	

A Good List update


Last week I wrote about The Good List, my new newsletter that offers ways to add some joy to your days. The first installment went out this week <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2F1JusaJmGCJs1wgQAkSx39w~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FHFoVe-zEfFF_T3dLRquKdPoT7GXSrY_94RtIX65lsuZHdV9cqNoOxn3H6c-iZI7w_5dyWA3zkH8harhnkVe01B0WMBH49SsMQK687-H24IBb-1i7dCRa-uKsL3CMaGbiNqQ26R0FstY4gmoA12LltlOXTfKArzTg95xTy8XSf2JmIhrFU9caiS2YaTLjxkWn894css-on55-JjKeNC4rH3owGNPak1eh8myZVs0ydKqXN-pNP5HKz6mC0_xNKARyi0-vP7f14PC6c-2dxMCnBQJzStiskFmMpVy0jg4z-RC6mQH0FdDlBaQq6R3wXodCvRlQq96XExZXcU2uNJ7-vx8D_5YrZcQJEZuun_z6faCx8J85H4os5uS7RhoFDoeZ&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C5b1e6071799b489c1f6f08de8730e77c%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096841303062269%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=GVYkvxFsvT7uus5SuWoIYK7E%2B1Yy4Yg3iuMJh%2FvoVQ4%3D&reserved=0> , and I’ve loved hearing from readers about how they cultivate delight in their own lives.

Jill Wiggins of Kerrville, Texas, wrote:

I am an 80-year-old widow who lives in the Texas Hill Country. In the past 10 years I have raised a grandchild (who is now on her own), cared for a husband who died of Parkinson’s, moved twice, had two major surgeries, plus of course the pandemic and the Big Texas Freeze of ’21.

When I take the dog for a walk on the beautiful Guadalupe River, I try to find at least five beautiful things. It can be birdsong, a cloud, the river itself, a flower, an egret, or even just my beautiful blue heeler. Once you start noticing, it’s easy to keep going and find way more than five, even on a not-so-pretty day.

Many skin care products promise miracles. Retinoids are among the few with the science to back them up. You've been invited to a webinar (Aether High Priority Projects) for Aether.


Webinar Details

*	Description: Please join us for live support with Aether's high priority projects! Office Hours are optional, but QMs will be available and happy to help with any questions.

*	Next Steps: Log in to your Outlier account to view available time slots and RSVP


Important Notes


*	Webinar attendance is always optional, but certain webinars offer participation incentives (listed in the event description).
*	Join the Zoom session with the same email address you use for Outlier so your attendance is recorded automatically.
*	If you must join with a different email, notify a project admin after the session so we can update your attendance
*	Incentives are awarded only once per webinar; you don’t need to attend again if you’ve already completed this session.

We look forward to seeing you online!

Thank you,

The Outlier Team

________________________________

From: Graham Mills
Sent: Thursday, March 19, 2026 8:25 PM
To: David, Isabella <isabella.david@ubs.com <mailto:isabella.david@ubs.com> >
Subject: Offer Letter Extension 

 

Hi Isabella,

 

Thank you again for extending the offer for the 2027 Summer Internship at UBS Asset Management. I am very excited about the opportunity and am thoroughly considering this next step in my career.

 

To ensure I can make the most informed decision, I would be grateful if you could grant me a short extension on the decision deadline. Would it be possible to have until Monday to provide my final answer? I was sick Monday and Tuesday and didn't really get the chance to speak with enough of the team, so the additional time to consider would help my decision-making process significantly.

 

Please let me know if this is feasible. I truly appreciate your understanding.

 

Best regards,

Graham Mills

Subject: Summer & part-time semester internship opportunities
Body:
Students: here is a summer internship opportunity with a start-up Private Equity firm in an interesting new niche.

	 

	Legal Enterprises of America ("LEA") is a newly launched private equity firm. It is the first platform solely dedicated to investing in law firms, an emerging asset class that is opening to private equity for the first time.

	 

	LEA serves as an investment and operating platform that will look for acquisitions, diligence investment opportunities, and improve portfolio companies, with substantial work focused on marketing and implementing technology.

	 

	LEA was founded by Brandon Foreman, a Duke alum who spent several years at Blackstone and Centerview Partners. Interested candidates will get the skills and experience needed to obtain and succeed in investment banking and investing roles similar to these, while candidates focused on operational and marketing roles will get hands-on experience that will be highly transferable. Internship roles may lead to full-time employment opportunities. 

	 

	Three separate roles are open, which may be part-time (during the school year) or summer only. Roles will be entirely virtual and may require 10-40 hours per week.

	1.	Investment Intern

	2.	Operations Intern

	3.	Marketing Intern

	Interested candidates should send an email to Brandon@ForemanEnterprises.com <mailto:Brandon@ForemanEnterprises.com>  with their resumes and the desired role specified in the subject line.

	 

	Thank you,

	Brandon

FutureEval: Measuring the Forecasting Accuracy of AI

First up: FutureEval <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fshtu1.mjt.lu%2Flnk%2FAWsAAJSLHhcAAc7jd_QAA_Tk4J0AAYKJHNAAoZUfAC0eXgBpvV3MrP2MuxD1Ti6UyGAETzaCvQApjyg%2F3%2F2C4-OMQP8CAtObjlDqzqxQ%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubWV0YWN1bHVzLmNvbS9mdXR1cmVldmFsLw&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C4877c98227cc44c335d708de868f7e48%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096148044756380%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=34qk2oN9x2rH6mmNktmLhCw%2FQJVJ6L%2FL9UJdREvxu3I%3D&reserved=0> , our benchmark that tracks how fast AI models are improving at predicting real-world events compared against human forecasters (both the general forecasting community and Metaculus Pro Forecasters). For those of you who followed our AI Forecasting Benchmark journey, FutureEval is the new home for this work.

You may have seen the recent buzz in TIME and The Atlantic around AI forecasting startups like Mantic and Lightning Rod (both tested on Metaculus). We're excited and curious about this fast-evolving field, which is why we created FutureEval. And by the way, we really do love hearing from you, so feel free to reply to this email with your thoughts!

Bots are improving, but Metaculus Pro Forecasters have beaten them in every season so far. For now, bots do best when forecasting on narrow questions; when the questions are complex and decision-relevant, they struggle. In tournaments such as Fiscal Showdown and Market Pulse, which included questions about U.S. fiscal policy or the future of specific government programs, for example, bot performance dropped dramatically.

 <https://shtu1.mjt.lu/img2/shtu1/b390c47c-ea64-4d32-921c-ab0aa131cc45/content> 	

The challenge lies in modeling relationships between multiple uncertain factors. These questions require reasoning about how policies, incentives, and external events interact, something current systems struggle to represent. These interconnections are key to forecasting that is genuinely useful for decision-makers, and they remain an area where human forecasters retain an advantage.

FutureEval's Competitive Advantage

Unlike traditional AI benchmarks, FutureEval evaluates whether AI can make reliable judgments about the future. Forecasting requires causal reasoning, planning, risk analysis, and an understanding of human behavior, making it a strong proxy for real-world intelligence.

FutureEval has several key advantages:

*	Real-world performance. Models forecast events whose outcomes are still unknown, eliminating test contamination.
*	Broad capabilities. Forecasting draws on decision-making, failure analysis, and social reasoning.
*	Scales with AI progress. Questions can grow longer-term and more complex.
*	Human + AI comparison. A live leaderboard compares models against both the community and Pro Forecasters.

How it works

We test major AI models live on Metaculus using forecasting questions with standardized prompts. As events resolve, we evaluate predictions using proper scoring rules measuring accuracy, calibration, and discrimination.

We're also tracking where bots "win" or "lose" against human predictions. It's still early, but some patterns are emerging.

"For forecasting that calls for high-speed, high-frequency updates, bots enjoy a natural advantage," Deger says. But for "questions where public information is sparse or judgments are more qualitative," Pro Forecasters outperform bots.

Why This Matters

Forecasting ability underpins decision-making across finance, policy, national security, and industry. Prediction markets alone saw over $44 billion in trading volume last year. What happens when markets begin relying on AI systems capable of making more accurate predictions than even the best human forecasters?

We're also excited for FutureEval to function as a hub for researchers and builders developing next-generation forecasting systems. Shape the Future of Scientific Funding in the ARIA Horizon Scanning Tournament

Are you a scientist or researcher working in plant biotech, biomanufacturing, genomics, ecosystems, biodefense, regulatory science, or related fields? This tournament may be for you.

Pinpointing the most consequential research domains amid shifting scientific, market, and geopolitical landscapes is one of the hardest problems in science funding. This new tournament is part of the Horizon Scanning Study Group (HSSG), a collaboration between Renaissance Philanthropy, the UK's Advanced Research + Invention Agency (ARIA), and Metaculus.

ARIA empowers scientists and engineers to pursue breakthroughs at the edge of the possible. Renaissance Philanthropy and Metaculus helped convene the HSSG: assembling cross-disciplinary experts, hosting workshops, and developing forecasting questions mapping research bottlenecks and opportunities.

Your forecasts will help quantify uncertainty and inform where ARIA focuses next, offering a rare chance to impact real scientific funding decisions.

Sample questions include:

*	Will thale cress, maize, and soybean achieve 50% faster transformation-to-T1 seed timelines before 2030?
*	What percentage of survey respondents in the 2031 Eurobarometer on Food Safety will say they are concerned about GMOs?
*	How many seed plant species will have structurally annotated genomes before 2030?
*	When will the first precision-bred organism be commercially authorised in the UK?

Join the Junior Residential Board (JRB) for our Study Abroad Panel to hear from our juniors who have been there and get all your questions answered!
We will also have catering from Zweli's. Register below!

Whose war?


What does the United States want to achieve in its nearly three-week war on Iran? What does Israel? At the start of the conflict, the two countries seemed to share similar goals: topple the leader, enfeeble the military and forever terminate the nuclear program.

Now, though, the allies seem to be diverging, my colleague Steven Erlanger reports <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FvVJQ1EAaF5VOjLw4o1G_Uw~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FrAC5yHs83t4K_fBJLUJ-HfTqZrgc-rDGhVy4GSQqsbnLZcqKxfnivuVBCNNCh32sy6Q-SnZKtjT4SrDiLK-IH764cCyz9o-cdP7HaOIvXgUdPrlsJvhktDhLQGApYP67qLnoJlmVHNp9JkZxzStTD6jG0Xq6eYYYa584clr5jZ4n8yWZ2PSSwCeeqZqyny1lpvazI0305P8ArdRtjIcv1hvDAXm36i8CNNiVhhItFhyF3Pj223rVgVRdpe35j67hozfuYoonmhuc9c5Et8TTOYDph1xRvoMgEdbW2WSFUAnp0WTHT8gz65ViuHkLCZNhUomzMwG9AJr5dN2Mvix3mLQvUo45qzpJbnh6IJEjYyfSf2QNdRBtoMjFTQ-6rjOu&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd104c5725922480798be08de86704bb3%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096014088416455%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=5Vp7GwiFyCFMrlP1%2BW3CrM6LNXQnSt3Hfkbg0Gaf9D0%3D&reserved=0> . For all the rhetoric we remember about America First, the United States remains a global superpower concerned about the worldwide supply of oil and the safety of its allies around the Persian Gulf. Iran does not pose an existential threat to Washington, and America’s leaders don’t want their voters impoverishing themselves at the gas pump.

Israel, however, is a regional power. Its concerns are narrower. Put simply, it wants to cripple a country that has sworn itself to Israel’s destruction. So it keeps killing officials in Tehran, grinding down the government, blowing up oil facilities and striking Iran’s proxy, Hezbollah. “It sees an extraordinary opportunity to clobber Iran with American help, and it is likely to want to continue the war longer than President Trump,” Steve writes.

The Islamic Republic has retaliated against energy targets in the Gulf and sent global oil and gas prices soaring. If it keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed and induces a global recession, well, that’s not Israel’s worry, analysts say. “They have a set of strategic objectives and believe they are succeeding, and they’re not as price sensitive as the White House,” one Iran expert told Steve. “They are more willing to weather the storm and try to finish the job.”

A former Pentagon official put it succinctly: “Most Israelis simply hope for the demise of their nemesis,” he said.

The fear in Washington


The Trump administration understands that Americans, for whom the stakes are lower, will have less patience than Israelis. The president wants to reassure people. “It will be over with pretty soon,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office yesterday.

Until then, his aides are trying to salve the economic wounds. Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, said the U.S. could release more oil from its strategic reserves. And he told Fox Business that the U.S. “may unsanction the Iranian oil” that is already at sea, about 140 million barrels. “That would, of course, bring more revenue to Iran,” my colleague David Sanger, who covers the White House, writes <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2FAVD5GHbCMWxiS2jaGiaU7g~~%2FAAAAARA~%2Fp2ofRjiGiNUbmqzQVec-Jhu2DOvYiSMF7_R6vMx05wYXCwxLEeU7m2pwJ-LG1rpi6ZFDj-XfP8dRc79BCCsELLJJF4NvVdKslRKgpVTv_dMCqHJ2t_0yTQRCpezy3SErY7VI2myuRWlmIeWxbyYK49Jh6l-FEVcnBZQqJU5_KmWWpvd-3Xtt_e_kTSzl49buocUmf3FYsLLmZ4tqB4BVcS94uwQJrM2RgHoyZToQsrPBmbOFWgdYjeBPa9quCMF56ixYnECwyIfmcuh8aj_xoCzsE1d3dS9Lk4Q3eOyGamZc4fgKlHlVciHKreBCrkxhuD3pidJ6_zpIDJXgv_d1BMyY7l9Y1v886WsNepAgobKDaJhaygCOBmVHYHE1Sdyg5Hdb27TBVYIy4au12jLjyw~~&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd104c5725922480798be08de86704bb3%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096014088429831%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=nLZzZIDaezFr8jMRP9bJyHmK4a75D9jYFhlUpeAtE1s%3D&reserved=0> . Bessent insisted, somewhat confusingly, that “we will be using the Iranian barrels against the Iranians to keep the price down.”

To finance that campaign, though, the Pentagon yesterday sent the White House a request for $200 billion in funding for the war — hardly a balm to those seeking a quick end. (“Obviously, it takes money to kill bad guys,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said.) Trump told reporters that such a sum would be “a small price to pay to make sure that we stay tippy top.” It’s also on par with what the United States spent annually at the height of the Iraq war.

Another fear in Washington, David reports, is that Gulf nations — which have not answered Iranian missile and drone attacks — will now begin to fight back. On Wednesday, two sets of incoming ballistic missiles were intercepted over Saudi Arabia, its defense ministry said. “We will not shy away from protecting our country and our economic resources,” the kingdom’s foreign minister said.

One Rattle After Another

 

Is the largest leveraged buyout ever in doubt?

 

A few weeks ago it looked like Paramount Skydance boss David Ellison was headed for a Hollywood ending <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44813946.467488%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9idXNpbmVzcy9tZWRpYS9lbGxpc29uLXdhcm5lci1wYXJhbW91bnQtZGVhbC1uZXRmbGl4LTIwNmUzZjM0P21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB52613f2c&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C25a9feb66f954192067508de866f7521%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096010768942223%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=CQ4VmMREAUQ4897nFb2tEAPhfntJUii%2BZ7rwdrlMbfU%3D&reserved=0>  with his courtship of Warner Bros. Now markets suggest he could face a delay, or worse.

 

Paramount stock is down 34% since it beat Netflix for the right to buy Warner for about $111 billion including debt. More interesting, though, is what has happened to Warner shares, which closed Thursday at $27.63.

 

A buyer who’s certain Paramount’s $31-a-share cash offer will be paid by the end of September, when a “ticking fee” starts accruing, can snag an annualized 20% return buying Warner stock today. That’s much higher than the usual payoff for all cash takeovers. Merger arbitrage traders boost that with borrowed money, so why are they wary?

 

Media analyst Rich Greenfield, co-founder of LightShed Partners, reckons the deal will only close early next year. Since the ticking fee is modest, a delay actually would reduce an arbitrager’s return.

 

But Ellison moves quickly. A person familiar with the deal’s financing and regulatory hurdles expressed confidence that it would be done by September.

 

Paramount would have a bitter pill to swallow if regulators actually blocked the transaction. That would trigger a $7 billion termination fee, in addition to the $2.8 billion the media company already paid indirectly to Netflix <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44813946.467488%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9idXNpbmVzcy9tZWRpYS9uZXRmbGl4LWRlYWwtd2FybmVyLWJyb3MtZGlzY292ZXItM2IzM2IwMmM_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBb8bc5455&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C25a9feb66f954192067508de866f7521%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096010769030154%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=DQpKrLl%2BFSTVHLaxlwatb4fHLbPDkSe%2BRIUVKWXuVOI%3D&reserved=0> . Paramount’s entire market value is now below $10 billion.

 

Outright rejection seems unlikely, though, and money seems no obstacle. David Ellison’s dad, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, is one of the world’s richest people. He personally guaranteed that a family trust providing much of the equity financing would follow through.

 

That might have been with the expectation, though, that sovereign-wealth funds <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44813946.467488%2FaHR0cHM6Ly92YXJpZXR5LmNvbS8yMDI2L2ZpbG0vbmV3cy9wYXJhbW91bnQtd2FybmVyLWJyb3MtbmF0aW9uYWwtc2VjdXJpdHktcmV2aWV3LWFyYWItd2VhbHRoLWZ1bmRzLXdhcnJlbi1ibHVtZW50aGFsLTEyMzY2ODEwNjcvP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB2c00d8c9&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C25a9feb66f954192067508de866f7521%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096010769046530%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=UsN8Rtu7tEkJN5RLKrOKMZfi7wJnE0RiIDOioOk75Vg%3D&reserved=0>  from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi would share the risk. They pledged $24 billion to an earlier offer.

 

Unfortunately, the takeover battle was won just hours before the Iran war <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44813946.467488%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS93b3JsZC9taWRkbGUtZWFzdC9lc2NhbGF0aW5nLWF0dGFja3Mtb24tZ3VsZi1lbmVyZ3ktYXNzZXRzLXBsdW5nZS1pcmFuLXdhci1pbnRvLW5ldy1waGFzZS0zNmNjMGE2ZT9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB344f3f78&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C25a9feb66f954192067508de866f7521%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096010769061752%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=S4luifQ81VyISYaciUqtmR7oV5KQCa%2FuhG%2Fo1p%2FPUmA%3D&reserved=0>  turned their financial worlds upside down <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44813946.467488%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9idXNpbmVzcy90aGUtdHJpbGxpb25zLW9mLWRvbGxhcnMtb2YtdS1zLWludmVzdG1lbnQtYXQtc3Rha2UtaW4tdGhlLWd1bGYtZjY2Zjc4ODM_bW9kPWRqZW1NYXJrZXRzQU0%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBffe223e5&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C25a9feb66f954192067508de866f7521%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096010769076928%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=qb8jPhDsNMxYy1wwjt9ZIOEdl5y44JsF45T0JSDeW1Q%3D&reserved=0> . Might they write smaller checks or bow out entirely if the conflict drags on?

 

There’s a worrying precedent from the financial crisis of a big American company being left in the lurch. Dow Chemical flirted with ruin <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44813946.467488%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9hcnRpY2xlcy9CTC1MQi03ODI3P21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB1c0ba743&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C25a9feb66f954192067508de866f7521%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096010769091271%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=4iugdUxRbojpACGGypR%2FYa15mPy3FbrVuHNJ33FtO2Y%3D&reserved=0>  because it won a bidding war for a competitor in 2008 but was left billions short at closing time when a Kuwaiti state company backed out <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44813946.467488%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9hcnRpY2xlcy9TQjEyMzA0ODU2NTE5NzQzNzgxNz9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB38120b0b&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C25a9feb66f954192067508de866f7521%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639096010769105568%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=OYmIik5ARbox5oBeZkQWpclwJa%2BKeAcUFSc2cY0mXrw%3D&reserved=0>  of a joint venture.

 

Given the prestige of this deal and the Ellisons’ closeness to President Trump, not to mention a unique family backstop, the money should be there one way or another. Even that won’t be the end of Paramount’s problems since it will have to unlock hefty synergies to whittle down a mountain of debt.

 

But current Warner shareholders will have cash in their pockets by then and can watch the show from the cheap seats.

This New York congressional race is turning into a bitter AI war. 


Artificial-intelligence companies have pledged about $265 million for super PACs and similar groups ahead of this year’s midterm elections. One big AI PAC is targeting Alex Bores, a computer scientist and New York state assemblyman who is running to represent a congressional district that covers much of Manhattan. Hi,




Congratulations! We are thrilled to offer you a seat in our Spring 2026 Project Destined Real Estate Private Equity Virtual Internship Program. Your application stood out from a competitive pool of 3,000+ applicants, and we were impressed by your background, and enthusiasm for launching your career in Real Estate Private Equity.




As part of the 5-week program, you will join a distinguished cohort of over 150+ students from 60+ universities and 20+ global cities. Together, you will gain the skills, knowledge, and relationships needed to secure your first investment property or a role in private equity, investment banking, capital markets, or related fields.




The program focuses on three key goals:

1.	Building skills and experiences to enhance your resume, LinkedIn profile and engage top firms.

2.	Strengthening both your technical and “power” skills (communication, teamwork, and leadership).

3.	Preparing you to excel in interviews for competitive roles in real estate private equity and to build analyses for your own (future) investment opportunities. 

	
	

The core elements of the program include:

*	Live Weekly Training Sessions: Led by Cedric Bobo, (Project Destined’s Founder and CEO, and former Carlyle Group Executive) and other industry leaders, sessions will teach you how to build financial projections, value properties, raise capital, and analyze investment returns.

*	Networking Opportunities: Build relationships with executives in Real Estate Private Equity, Investment Banking, Capital Markets, and more. 

*	Team Activities and Live Deal Competition: Work with peers to evaluate investment opportunities and compete in a live deal competition.

*	Presentation / Interview Training: Gain skills to thrive in interviews and prepare you to secure capital for your own investment property.  

*	Opportunity for Scholarship Stipend: Top students will have the opportunity to earn a scholarship stipend based on program performance, competitions, attendance and completion of deliverables. 

	
	

Onboarding Activities:

*	You will receive an email one week before the program begins with your calendar invites and access to your Monday.com Student Activity Board to help you stay engaged and on track.

	
	

To confirm your spot, please complete the acceptance form linked here <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fprojectdestined.us17.list-manage.com%2Ftrack%2Fclick%3Fu%3D6a7623e661b782123cb167aba%26id%3D7079259d2e%26e%3Dfe75a3a393&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C713af91a0d724147b43408de73ad19a5%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639075384496237300%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=mqnkv%2Bce13hJ%2BiQzVSCvPjSVfV9UyHqf71EwjAVa5fo%3D&reserved=0>  by February 28th on or before 5:00 PM ET.

Subject: Duke University-Budget Shortfall in Nelnet Payment Plan
Body:
Bursar's Office- Student Accounts       

                    


February 24, 2026

Dear Graham, 




Our records show that you are participating in the NELNET payment plan.  As of today, it appears that there is a shortfall in your budget for the 2026 Spring Term.  Your current account balance for the semester will not be cleared by the NELNET payments we anticipate being made through April 1, 2026.  




Credits in future terms should not be included in the Nelnet budget and are not factored into the amount due for the Spring semester.




This amount is based on:

*	your current account balance,

*	new charges that may have been added to your account,

*	any pending financial aid (aid not yet posted to your student account), and

*	your remaining NELNET payments: note you may view your NELNET account online at https://mycollegepaymentplan.com/duke/ <https://mycollegepaymentplan.com/duke/> or by logging into DukeHub.




Please use the DukeHub <https://dukehub.duke.edu/>  website to verify that all your financial aid appears correctly on your account.  If you have aid that has not yet posted, please check your financial aid information on DukeHub <https://dukehub.duke.edu/>  to see if there are remaining actions needed to complete the financial aid award process.  If you have questions about your aid package, please contact your financial aid office.




If you have authorized a NELNET payer, they have not received a copy of this email.  Please share this information with them.




To ensure that your future term registration is not restricted, your Nelnet plan must be adjusted to clear your Duke Bursar balance as of the final draft on April 1, 2026.




If there is additional information regarding payments and/or financial aid that you feel we have not considered, please contact us at bursar@duke.edu <mailto:bursar@duke.edu>  or the Bursar's office by phone at (919) 684-3531. 




Thank you for your attention to this matter.




With regards,

Your tariff questions


We knew that you would have questions about Friday’s Supreme Court decision invalidating President Trump’s tariff regime. He has already invoked a new law — the Trade Act of 1974 — to impose a flat 15 percent tariff on imports, but that expires in five months unless Congress extends it. Now he is exploring provisions that target unfair trading practices and national security threats <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnl.nytimes.com%2Ff%2Fnewsletter%2F6qoyvVe_9pi7_ZR2ZeGslw~~%2FAAAAARA~%2FDcYDnlmoC_2ncBQmbQSP88q286bc1X1WToFAVb6I-uBCFNDSL7Etye7g_qqQuPtlDj5dBJHjvluhq9hhJjzFoa_Rwyy9GTSLNAgUwTy8bYxp_JWylwNzESSsxFVnBm5lyYroFUfIv42u0MbwEFPCx8Qf5crRRc8QSDqiHfNg-UxmDPGjTn0zlQApyVqQE6xPPCahDutHa0ZhvzZNxMRzsyroi7wZLB5bEy8EaEBCELZQLnb6uVpAqX85BWzq4X3nctKkLMBmDP_CfLvFGq0a3D21YdqqscCfMRjGXWM-lZp2wejAw1WPnFf8AHj4-GivHqq-QQjIJs-xWSwQhkytG4NieA8zjVenH6xB6PJwLyoqjJLGDLZvb1M4ThH19sF1&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C4f68b7bcc79348f66b6d08de739b4039%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639075307814880685%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=aL7SAQlNyXyj8a2I02%2FNtK%2F9G8rpY1jGhLxBsZEp9Pk%3D&reserved=0> .

But what happens to the companies that paid steep levies? What will Trump do next? Should you pay your personal tariff bill? We brought your questions to expert Times reporters.


Economic effects


Please tell us how this ruling will affect average Americans. What price changes are we likely to see? How soon? | Renée Pesheck, Ann Arbor, Michigan

Lydia DePillis, who covers the economy, writes:

Probably not much. Companies would rather not lower prices once consumers have gotten used to them. Plus, Trump has already imposed those 15 percent tariffs across the board. Economists estimate the average effective tariff rate will go down by only about one percentage point. Still, you might see some relief on items that come from countries that had the highest tariffs, like India and Brazil — certain spices and nuts, for example.

Are any impacts of Trump’s tariffs permanent or irreversible? | Arielle Zabusky, Durham, North Carolina

Ben Casselman, The Times’s chief economics correspondent, writes:

Almost certainly, but it’s hard to know exactly what those impacts are just yet. Many companies have changed their supply chains and shifted production to different countries. Those shifts will be difficult to reverse. For the economy more broadly, trade flows will eventually adapt to whatever tariff regime takes hold. But both major political parties have turned their back on the free-trade orthodoxy that was dominant in earlier decades, and corporations are adjusting their business models to reflect that reality.

What is the money raised by the tariffs earmarked for? Who has oversight on how it is spent? | Samantha Dennis, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania

Andrew Duehren, who covers taxes, writes:

It’s not earmarked for anything in particular. Like other tax revenue, money raised from tariffs is deposited in the Treasury General Account — basically the checking account for the federal government. So, despite the way Trump has sometimes talked about the tariff revenue, it’s not a special pot of money that the administration can deploy however it sees fit. Congress decides and oversees federal spending.


Refunds


Many businesses now say the government should refund the levies they paid. Who has the ultimate authority to determine if, how and when companies would get refunds? | John Royse, Bridgman, Michigan

Ana Swanson, who covers trade, writes:

The Supreme Court left this issue to lower courts and the U.S. Court of International Trade, a separate federal court that deals with customs issues. It’s unclear whether they will order refunds, what the process would look like or how long it would take to play out. If refunds happen, Customs and Border Protection and the Treasury Department will need to set up a system to refund money, and it could take months or even years to get money back. Violence raged across Mexico after its military killed a powerful cartel boss, Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho. His supporters wreaked havoc in at least a dozen states, blocking roads and setting fire to supermarkets, banks and vehicles. At least 62 people were killed in the fighting.

Who was El Mencho? He was the head of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. The criminal organization expanded rapidly under his leadership, producing and selling drugs, extorting local businesses and terrorizing communities.

History is littered with new technologies that led to stock-market booms and busts. Artificial intelligence is different: This year it’s providing boom and bust at the same time.

 

There’s a boom in spending on data centers and research to support AI. There’s a bust both in the shares of companies that might (perhaps) be replaced by AI and, to a lesser extent, in shares of firms paying for those data centers.

 

It feels contradictory, but has a logic. Generative AI feels like magic: It can churn out a sales strategy or write a haiku about yogurt. The poetry is so-so, but programmers are entranced by its coding skill.

 

Lots of companies might find their business models undermined if it’s quick and easy to create new software. There’s been a crash in the S&P 500 software and services sector, which intensified Monday.

 

The apparent contradiction is that shares of companies selling the AI tools are also struggling. Microsoft is down 21% this year. Amazon, a big investor in unlisted Anthropic and operator of the largest cloud service, is off 11%. Alphabet and Meta have gone nowhere.

 

The explanation is that investors are worried about the scale of their AI spending. Fund managers told a regular Bank of America survey they are more concerned about overinvestment <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F44303449.460264%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9saXZlY292ZXJhZ2Uvc3RvY2stbWFya2V0LXRvZGF5LWRvdy1zcC01MDAtbmFzZGFxLTAyLTE3LTIwMjYvY2FyZC9hLXRvcC1uZXctY29uY2Vybi1mb3ItZnVuZC1tYW5hZ2Vycy1jb21wYW5pZXMtYXJlLW92ZXJpbnZlc3RpbmctLUF2M1BSM2hnNDdOWWZiaDFkeVZkP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB3f3325c1&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C018ac0d1aa2c436f2a2208de73978693%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639075291819698423%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Ce4vQQ4P8PSxQJPX5qHhdGGJjUYbMBCoAWBCvh1vm4w%3D&reserved=0>  than underinvestment by companies for the first time.

 

Greater capital expenditure requires higher profits to justify the investment. Yet, the more capex committed by Big Tech, the more competition there will be between rival AI platforms. That could lower prices—not great for future profits.

 

Worse, companies that had been capital light and cash rich, generating high margins in winner-takes-all markets, are becoming capital heavy and indebted. The idea of lower returns on capital, big spending and more competition is less appealing. Oracle, borrowing a lot compared with its size, has fallen 28% this year.

 

The winners from this spending should be users, who get more AI more cheaply. But it’s much easier to identify the companies selling the stuff needed to build or fill all the new data centers.

 

Caterpillar and GE Vernova, which benefit from building and powering the centers, are up 32% and 27%, respectively. Makers of the memory and testing kit needed have led the market amid shortages: Sandisk is up 181%, Western Digital 63% and Seagate Technology 48%.

 

The biggest chip stocks, led by Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD, have been flat to down this year. Other names such as Dutch chip-making equipment manufacturer ASML have helped power the semiconductor sector to a 18% gain.

 

Markets make their best guess as to the winners and losers, but the scale and speed of the combined boom and bust makes me queasy. These bets could reverse rapidly, while the ultimate winners—and the risk of a normal historical bust—remain impossible to predict.

Luxury brands struggle in booming resale market

 

The market for secondhand luxury goods is approaching a tipping point, but many brands can’t decide which way to jump. 

 

Last year, the value of the luxury resale market hit 50 billion euros for the first time, based on estimates from Bain & Company, equivalent to $59 billion at current exchange rates. Tonight, President Trump will use his State of the Union address to sell the public on the economy and unveil new measures meant to lower costs <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gdkjko-hrkusddg-h%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ceefa1f0a5c854babaf4508de7396a134%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639075287963738426%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7FKbrt30%2FXAsQw9pSGwspwwxdtZnfAbypVXy6PgXY9o%3D&reserved=0> , as Republicans try to address voters’ concerns ahead of the midterm elections later this year. With Trump on the back foot after a stinging judicial rebuke of his power to impose tariffs, Xi Jinping is spying a chance to reset relations with the U.S. on Beijing’s terms ahead of Trump’s trip to China, scheduled for March 31 to April 2. Chief China correspondent Lingling Wei writes about how the battleground of the U.S.-China trade fight has suddenly shifted <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gdkjko-hrkusddg-yk%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Ceefa1f0a5c854babaf4508de7396a134%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639075287964116896%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=5FTqyXG9Jr76tq9ZMfNEbTnh2Rz9BS3B%2BDRSjPVRO6U%3D&reserved=0> .

A: The Supreme Court has effectively dismantled the cornerstone of Trump’s trade strategy, ruling that the White House can’t use emergency powers as a blank check to levy broad, across-the-board tariffs. By stripping away these duties, the court has deprived the president of his preferred weapon of economic pressure just weeks before he lands in Beijing for a summit with the Chinese leader.

The impact on the ground is immediate. The effective U.S. tariff rate on Chinese goods will tumble from 32% to 23%, according to Capital Economics. This drop reflects the administration’s new—albeit temporary—15% global tariff rate, a fallback the administration reached for immediately after the ruling.

As a result, China emerges as the biggest winner of this shift so far, according to Capital Economics. As the import duty on Chinese goods shrinks, the incentive for companies to move production to other parts of Asia diminishes.

Yet, Trump still holds formidable tools to squeeze Beijing, from blocking the sale of advanced chips, jet engines and other high-tech gear to threatening new tariffs over Beijing’s failure to meet past trade promises, namely the commitments struck under a trade agreement during Trump’s first presidency.

Award Nominations Now Open


Each year, Duke University honors members of the Duke community whose actions reflect integrity, generosity, and a deep dedication to serving others through two distinguished awards:

✨ Lars Lyon Volunteer Service Award <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ft.e2ma.net%2Fclick%2F8p3z8l%2Fkrs9h54c%2F077c93&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd25917b2292f49b8daac08de731de08f%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639074769326803146%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=lHwsepTYsgOfw5A0TkqI3CCDB%2F6ghV5a0z6U6sEe05U%3D&reserved=0> 
✨ Algernon Sydney Sullivan Award <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ft.e2ma.net%2Fclick%2F8p3z8l%2Fkrs9h54c%2Fg08c93&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd25917b2292f49b8daac08de731de08f%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639074769326840707%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Ep5Dej9QVcaj18mDzmYTNyKJxqxdDgdtHiWy9M5rpy4%3D&reserved=0> 

These awards celebrate individuals who lead with humility, show up consistently for their communities, and create meaningful, lasting impact beyond their academic or professional roles. 

 <https://d31hzlhk6di2h5.cloudfront.net/20260223/96/6b/78/2e/3c7543eba0fb4ab6ce32b87f.jpg> 

Algernon Sydney Sullivan Award 


The Algernon Sydney Sullivan Award honors individuals who demonstrate exemplary character, integrity, and a deep commitment to serving others. 

Duke University gives this award annually to recognize members of the Duke community who have demonstrated generosity of character and acted as humble community members, placing service to others before self-interest.  

This award recognizes: 

 • One graduating senior

 • One graduate or professional student (House Staff included) 

 • One faculty or staff member 

Qualities and contribution to others should be practically applied to daily living, distinct from academic and professional achievements.  

Strong nominations have multiple letters of support and can be submitted either as one nomination or multiple nominations. We particularly welcome nominations of individuals who have not been previously recognized for their contributions to the community. 

Nomination Form <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ft.e2ma.net%2Fclick%2F8p3z8l%2Fkrs9h54c%2Fws9c93&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd25917b2292f49b8daac08de731de08f%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639074769326859660%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=QBpg1Zxqj3ejgTXH0LO4V%2FNF58NlBX3yXcBdEIg2fOU%3D&reserved=0> 

Lars Lyon Volunteer Service Award


The Lars Lyon Volunteer Service Award recognizes a rising sophomore, junior, or senior at Duke who has made a meaningful difference through service with a local school or nonprofit organization.

The recipient will receive a $20,000 partial scholarship to be applied toward tuition for the following academic year.

To be considered, undergraduates must have exhibited a strong dedication to service while at Duke and must be nominated by a member of the faculty or staff, a fellow student, or a representative of a Durham non-profit or public school. 

Established in 1989, the award honors the life and values of Lars Lyon, a Duke undergraduate remembered for his generosity, compassion, and dedication to volunteer service. Nominees reflect this same spirit through sustained engagement, leadership, and a genuine commitment to serving others.

Subject: Data Fest 2026 will take place March 20-22.  Undergrads, Sign up now!
Body:
Hi all,

I am writing to announce ASA DataFest 2026 at Duke. ASA DataFest at Duke is organized by the Department of Statistical Science at Duke University and will take place in Perkins Library on Duke University West Campus, Friday March 20 through Sunday March 22.
DataFest is a data analysis competition where teams of up to five students attack a large, complex, and surprise data set over a weekend. Your job is to represent your school by finding and communicating insights into these data. The teams that impress the judges will win prizes as well as glory for their school. Everyone will have a great experience, lots of food, and fun!
The event is open to all undergraduate students, regardless of level of programming experience. In previous years, first year students who have only taken introductory statistics courses won awards and prizes. Additionally, in anticipation of the event weekend,  Duke’s Center for Data and Visualization Sciences will host pre-event workshops. See the DataFest website for more details: https://dukestatsci.github.io/datafest/ <https://dukestatsci.github.io/datafest/> 

Whether you form a team or wish to be assigned a team, registration is open! You can sign up here: https://dukestatsci.github.io/datafest/#signup <https://dukestatsci.github.io/datafest/#signup> 

Are you a Master’s or PhD student looking to get involved as a consultant? Please fill out the consultant form on the signups page above.

Please reach out to Dr. Alexander Fisher (alexander.fisher@duke.edu) with any questions.

We hope to see you there!


Alexander Fisher, Ph.D
Assistant Professor of the Practice
Department of Statistical Science, Duke University







Forwarded for DataFest!   

Joan Combs Durso, Ph.D.

Coordinator of Undergraduate Training, Research, and Development

Department of Statistical Science, 

Trinity College of Arts and Sciences, Duke University

Subject: Open House THIS Week - Blue Light + 300 Swift
Body:
<https://duke.campusgroups.com/read/b364bde7-10f4-11f1-bd1c-025c6e3d0caf.png> Hello Class of 2028!  

We’re excited to invite you to two open houses this week! They are both great opportunities to explore our HRL apartment communities, enjoy themed activities, and get a feel for the general spaces in each complex. Specific room tours will take place in March, but these events will give you a solid first look at what each location has to offer!

________________________________


🔵 Blue Light Open House – Book Swap


Date: February 24th
Time: 7:00–9:00 PM

Bring a book to swap (or grab one even if you forget!) and enjoy a cozy, community‑centered evening while checking out the Blue Light building and its amenities. This is a great chance to see the overall space before room tours begin next month.
 <https://duke.campusgroups.com/upload/duke/2026/flyer_image_upload_4215721_BL_Open_House_223151518.jpg> 

________________________________


🎨 300 Swift Open House – Paint & Sip


Date: February 26
Time: 7:30 PM

Join us for a relaxing Paint & Sip night at 300 Swift! While you paint and enjoy refreshments, you’ll also have the chance to tour the shared spaces and learn more about living in the Swift community. Specific room tours will be offered in March.

 <https://duke.campusgroups.com/upload/duke/2026/flyer_image_upload_4215721_300_Swift_Open_House__223151540.png> 

________________________________

Whether you're exploring future housing options or simply want to get a feel for each community, we’d love to see you at one or both of these events!

Feel free to reach out with any questions.




Residence Life 

Duke University
