SELL?

 

Don’t say you weren’t warned. Repeatedly.

 

Michael Burry, the fund manager played by Christian Bale in “The Big Short,” compared recent, frenetic tech-stock action to the “scene of the bloody car crash, minutes before it happens” in a Substack post <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly9zdWJzdGFjay5jb20vaG9tZS9wb3N0L3AtMTk3MTc2ODUyP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB255fd780&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928044916%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=9pC6FSXawGRE8bHeqjS3NLBQ8RL2qFnaOvt6WUi2%2B3c%3D&reserved=0>  this week. He recommended selling stocks in the market’s hottest corners.

 

Burry goes by the moniker “Cassandra Unchained <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly94LmNvbS9taWNoYWVsamJ1cnJ5P21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBf220a9da&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928086706%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=rsipFv6dup6xGkH4uI9bewaij3RJZwonHOTEdvzEeKs%3D&reserved=0> ” on social media. Since the epic housing bet that made him famous, though, he’s been the inverse of that mythological princess. She was cursed with seeing the future but not being believed.

 

Burry, whose firm didn’t respond to emails, has received lots of media attention <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9maW5hbmNlL3N0b2Nrcy9taWNoYWVsLWJ1cnJ5LWJldHMtaGUtaXNudC10b28tZWFybHktdG8tZ28tYWdhaW5zdC10aGUtYWktanVnZ2VybmF1dC01ZDk1ZDIxZT9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB797484ab&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928105895%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=yE4ccAyFsA%2BnO57kUcCjh5jl49AH4y7kG%2BbrFQH6zpY%3D&reserved=0>  for his often-cryptic warnings. He famously tweeted “SELL” in January 2023 before deleting his X account. In 2022, he wondered whether an economic downturn could be “worse than 2008.” And he warned about a “bubble” in passive investing in September 2019.

 

Even for those not managing money, the financial and emotional rewards from predicting a calamity are large. Consider Roger Babson, who got rich off of investing newsletters in the 1920s and 1930s. He ran for president in 1940, endowed an eponymous college and launched a foundation to overcome gravity <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubmV3Ym9zdG9uaGlzdG9yaWNhbHNvY2lldHkuY29tL2dyYXZpdHkuaHRtbD9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB668543d3&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928124548%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=vBcVVaamSmIQ1sa2XJ86zrTZqWgYHQQ7KqWUg19%2BkGo%3D&reserved=0> .

 

Babson warned about the Crash of 1929 six weeks before it happened. He also alerted subscribers to the Crashes of 1927 and 1928. You probably haven’t heard of those since they didn’t happen.

 

Elaine Garzarelli, who predicted a stock-market plunge in a TV interview shortly before the 1987 crash, became the best-paid strategist on Wall Street. But she went on to have a lackluster track record <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly9yaXRob2x0ei5jb20vMjAxNC8wNy90b2RheS1pbi0xOTk0LWdhcnphcmVsbGktZnVuZC1jbG9zZWQvP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB03d853ea&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928143594%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=beVybCX5r76jzsLaEmhjwiC7o31YDoWuUzi9AsMYE9U%3D&reserved=0> . Newsletter writer Robert Prechter correctly predicted the epic bull market in 1982 but then multiple wipeouts that never occurred <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9hcnRpY2xlcy9TQjEwMDAxNDI0MDUyNzQ4NzA0Nzk5NjA0NTc1MzU2ODQwNTMzNzM0MTgyP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBd430e95f&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928162181%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=i7WMEvdSkKTJQhpPq%2B0pUoaxTHh0IX0hCzi5fb97tfg%3D&reserved=0> . 

 

In fairness, Burry is no one-trick pony—his stock picks often have been brilliant. And, ahem, regular readers of Markets A.M. will recall lots of hand-wringing about tech stocks when prices were lower. “He who lives by the crystal ball learns to eat ground glass,” as they say.

 

In his Substack post, Burry resented being called “the boy who cried wolf,” saying the media has “misread regulatory filings” and has said he was calling for a “crash” when he didn’t use the word. Sure enough, some headlines <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45688997.406455%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmxvb21iZXJnLmNvbS9uZXdzL2FydGljbGVzLzIwMjYtMDUtMTEvbWljaGFlbC1idXJyeS13YXJucy1vZi1zdG9jay1jcmFzaC1hcy10ZWNoLWp1bXAtZWNob2VzLTIwMDAtcGVhaz9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBc0b71e33&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cd2f35582a8a94b26bd8308deb0dbb873%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142654928179751%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=xpVS6W02ah8K1IPA1pEn%2BuRHFvccr9LCMjrm6aPjFXk%3D&reserved=0>  this week did. 

 

Unlike Babson, who said he used Newtonian physics to divine the direction of the market, there’s real market logic behind Burry’s latest call. He skewers the line that tech stocks are reasonably priced on forward earnings. On the basis of “owners’ earnings,” a measure favored by Warren Buffett, he says the Nasdaq-100’s forward multiple is about 40% higher than reported.

 

None of that means stocks are about to plunge. If they do, the boost to Burry’s renown will outweigh the consequences of being too early again.

His nighttime missives on Truth Social—sometimes 50-plus posts overnight—offer a rare window into what the world’s most powerful man is thinking about. We analyzed thousands of Trump’s posts <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gutdrtk-hrkusddg-i%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cacc6efd28fa64f6c7fb408deb0d9f3ee%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142647325032719%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Za8znVOJ0aLdMm9x7F6cLYBJrxThrN%2BlmwFsLmg1YMI%3D&reserved=0>  and found that the president uses the social-media platform to spread conspiracy theories, attack his adversaries and amplify his frustrations about immigration, crime and more.

Emma Tucker
Editor in Chief, The Wall Street Journal

1

*	Jho Low, the alleged mastermind of one of the greatest financial frauds in history, is asking Trump <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gutdrtk-hrkusddg-d%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cacc6efd28fa64f6c7fb408deb0d9f3ee%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142647325054946%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=XgBTVm2lTkp8ZYRoQ%2BcMXgpcr73KU3r9IZATVszKZ1U%3D&reserved=0>  for a pardon.

Q: What do Trump and Xi want to achieve at their summit this week? 


Trump is scheduled to arrive in Beijing for a two-day visit that will include meetings with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The Journal’s Lingling Wei, Annie Linskey and Alexander Ward share what to expect <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail20.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gutdrtk-hrkusddg-s%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cacc6efd28fa64f6c7fb408deb0d9f3ee%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142647325575238%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=6YeehYl1jsHXpiJOw6QmdsneTIXhTbPaolAmSynsT0w%3D&reserved=0> : 

A: The summit will be the first presidential visit to China since Trump traveled there nearly nine years ago. Trump and Xi’s meeting comes as the Iran war looms over both countries, Trump targets Beijing’s partners in Venezuela and Cuba and as the U.S.-China relationship aims to recover from tit-for-tat economic brinkmanship last year.

Both leaders seek tangible wins. Trump, who is traveling with a delegation including Elon Musk, wants China to help end the Iran war and make big purchases of U.S. products. Xi, faced with a deepening economic slump at home, wants a more predictable relationship with Washington, as he works to erode its political and military commitments to Taiwan.

Each side is trying to reduce dependence on the other without rupturing the relationship that makes both economies work.

Behind closed doors, Trump treats Xi with a deference he rarely extends to other leaders, according to people familiar with their meetings.

U.S. officials and analysts expect Trump and Xi to repeat their usual displays of bonhomie but make few political breakthroughs in bilateral ties.

A major uncertainty hanging over the meeting is Taiwan, the self-governing democratic island Xi hopes to bring under Beijing’s fold. He is expected to try to press Trump to reduce the U.S.’s military support for the island.

Subject: An Update on the Canvas Security Incident
Body:
<https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ft.e2ma.net%2Fclick%2F5efgqh%2F1ry0blmb%2F1zkznp&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8ede761fc71447b19ae08deb0927071%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142340172013881%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=S3UaVQxRjmxoHXgEai%2BioMyIcFYiQ4FUommquFQOXvw%3D&reserved=0> 	
	
Dear faculty and students,
We’re writing to provide you with an update about the cybersecurity incident experienced by Canvas, which provides the university’s learning management system.  

That incident resulted in unauthorized access to data at Canvas from thousands of institutions, including Duke. As we shared with you on May 6 <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ft.e2ma.net%2Fclick%2F5efgqh%2F1ry0blmb%2Fhslznp&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8ede761fc71447b19ae08deb0927071%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142340172075079%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=%2BYQZLPs9geDmVLy6xdS%2BRRF%2BBaFP0jtC17dMD6idx8A%3D&reserved=0> , Instructure, the parent company for Canvas, says it has found no indication that passwords, dates of birth, government identifiers, or financial information were exposed in the incident. Updates on the breach and service disruption are available on Instructure's FAQ page <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ft.e2ma.net%2Fclick%2F5efgqh%2F1ry0blmb%2Fxkmznp&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8ede761fc71447b19ae08deb0927071%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142340172104483%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=qNJCfQzJYg712WdkZVCaytMgyRZSy6PTFT%2BS2UUE1IY%3D&reserved=0> .

Duke’s IT Security Office has reviewed an interim digital forensics report authored by a third-party security firm, which acknowledged the circumstances that led to the incident and included a statement that the bad actor is no longer present in the Instructure systems. Additionally, while we await further forensic information, the IT Security Office has credible evidence indicating that the following categories of Duke data at Canvas were affected: 

-- Names and contact information; 
-- Canvas’s internal usernames and account identifiers; 
-- Course and enrollments information (including sections and group membership); 
-- Course-related data (such as course details and cross-listings); 
-- Academic term information; 
-- Canvas account and school/unit information (including administrator usernames and observer information).
At this time, Duke’s IT Security Office review does not have evidence that grade information was accessed. 

As a precautionary measure, Duke has reinforced its digital security for all Canvas integrations with other services. In addition, the IT Security Office is monitoring all associated services and accounts closely. 
 
For the immediate and foreseeable future, Duke’s privacy office <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ft.e2ma.net%2Fclick%2F5efgqh%2F1ry0blmb%2Fddnznp&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cf8ede761fc71447b19ae08deb0927071%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142340172126241%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=NdV6wAyQ0V5gZkTxUu%2Fw7EPF6o97Sn6bQetGMrfl5tI%3D&reserved=0>  advises that students, faculty and staff may continue to use Canvas as an academic workspace but suggests serious caution when messaging or including any supplemental documentation on the platform related to sensitive personal information.  Sensitive personal information includes health details, accommodation requests and agreements, leave of absence requests and documentation, counseling received, and/or personal identifying information such as home address or birth date. 

Duke will continue to monitor the situation closely, and we will share additional guidance with you as new information becomes available. 
Thank you,

Nick Tripp
Chief Information Security Officer
Duke University

Subject: New Tasks - IG Video Conversations
Body:
<http://cdn.mcauto-images-production.sendgrid.net/764579af2201290d/2d0a7de9-228e-441e-8058-2c4cfdbca734/976x250.png> 


Hi Graham,




A new type of task will be available in Multimango soon. IG Video Conversations tasks focus on identifying pairs of real Instagram videos that already "communicate" with each other.





Purpose of the task


Your mission is to search through Instagram and find two videos where the second one naturally serves as a response or follow-up to the first. Once you identify these "input and response" pairs, you'll create a prompt based on them.





Key rules


• No creating: don't film or make your own content.

• No editing: don't change or cut the videos you find.

• Discovery only: your goal is to find videos that already exist "in the wild" and show how people react to one another.





Task types


There are several different relationships to look for:

• Reactions — a creator reacting to a viral clip.

• Covers or duets — someone doing their own version of a dance, song, or audio.

• Continuations — a follow-up post that builds on an earlier one ("how it started → how it's going").

• Behind-the-scenes — BTS footage paired with the polished final version.

• Parodies and response chains — a take that flips, mocks, or extends the original.




You're not limited to these — any case where the second video is a real and intentional response to the first one counts.





How to find a good pair


Start with the input video. Search Instagram for something someone might plausibly want a related video for: a viral moment, a popular dance, a recipe, a craft project, a sports highlight, etc.




Then find the related video. A few hunting tips by category:

• Reactions: check the original post's comments for @reactor mentions, then visit that person's profile.

• Covers and duets: tap the audio name on the original post — Instagram shows everyone who used that same audio, so the pair is right there.

• Behind-the-scenes: check the original creator's other recent posts, since BTS footage usually goes up around the same time as the final version.

• Continuations: look at the same creator's profile for follow-up posts (often labeled "part 2," "update," "the result," etc.). Multi-part reels also work — just trim them into two segments.





Writing the user prompt


Describe the desired output and how it differs from the input. Include text or label content, position, style, and timestamps when they apply.




• Good example: "Generate a video where @bob reacts to this — he should crack up at the punchline around 0:04, and add 'Mood: feral' as a yellow caption at the bottom from 0:02 to 0:06."

• Bad example: "Make a reaction."






Hard requirements


• Every video must come from Instagram — paste a permalink to a reel or video post.

• Each clip must be at least 4 seconds after trimming.

• Total video time (all inputs plus output combined, after trimming) must be 16 seconds or less.

• The final assistant turn must have exactly one video, the related response.

• The output must be a real, related response to the input, not just a random clip from the same genre or topic.

• Two trims from the same post are fine if they capture different moments (like "how it started → how it's going" from one reel).

• The user request must be at least 20 words and describe the change — what's in the output and how it connects to the input, not just a description of the input itself. Mention text, labels, and timestamps when they're relevant.





A note on quality


One great pair where the output genuinely responds to the input is worth ten generic pairs. If you find yourself struggling to explain why the output is "related," it probably isn't a strong match. Drop it and find a better one.

Subject: [Outlier Community] [Aether--Approved Annotators/Project Announcements] 📢 New Tasks - IG Video Conversations
Body:
<https://sea3.discourse-cdn.com/outliercommunity/user_avatar/community.outlier.ai/josafat_p_qm/45/1519648_2.png> 	Josafat_P_QM <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcommunity.outlier.ai%2Fu%2Fjosafat_p_qm&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C862959082447416d5ed208deb06d5fc2%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639142180988460696%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=w1Tugi%2BlELQYh96wiu38Taef3t74nA7tdrJGamP9ROI%3D&reserved=0>  
May 12 	

Hi team!  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/smile.png?v=15> 

A new type of task will be available in Multimango soon. The IG Video Conversations tasks will focus on identifying pairs of real Instagram videos that already “communicate” with each other.

________________________________


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/scroll.png?v=15> Purpose of the task


Your mission will be to search through Instagram and find two videos where the second one naturally serves as a response or follow-up to the first. Once you identify these “input and response” pairs, you will create a prompt based on them.


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/red_exclamation_mark.png?v=15> Key Rules


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/prohibited.png?v=15> No Creating: Do not film or make your own content.  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/video_camera.png?v=15> 
 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/prohibited.png?v=15> No Editing: Do not change or cut the videos you find.  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/scissors.png?v=15> 
 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/globe_showing_americas.png?v=15> Discovery Only: Your only goal is to find videos that already exist “in the wild” and show how people react to one another.  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/magnifying_glass_tilted_left.png?v=15> 


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/1234.png?v=15> Task Types


There will be different types of relationships to find, for example:

*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/open_mouth.png?v=15> Reactions 

	*	Example: A creator reacting to a viral clip.

*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/microphone.png?v=15> Covers/Duets 

	*	Example: Someone doing their own version of a dance, song, or audio.

*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/right_arrow.png?v=15> Continuations 

	*	Example: A follow-up post that builds on an earlier one (“how it started →how it’s going”)

*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/movie_camera.png?v=15> Behind-the-Scenes 

	*	Example: BTS footage paired with the polished final version.

*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/rofl.png?v=15> Parodies/Response Chains 

	*	Example: A take that flips, mocks, or extends the original.

You are not limited to these. Any option where the second video is a real and intentional response to the first video counts.


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/magnifying_glass_tilted_left.png?v=15> How to find a good pair


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/bullseye.png?v=15> Find your input video


Search for a video from Instagram and look for something someone might want a related video for: a viral moment, popular dance, recipes, craft projects, sports highlights, etc.


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/link.png?v=15> Find the related video


Hunting tips:

*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/open_mouth.png?v=15> Reactions: Check the original post’s comments for @reactor mentions, then visit that person’s profile
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/microphone.png?v=15> Covers/Duets: Tap the audio name on the original post — Instagram shows everyone who used that same audio. The pair is right there!
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/movie_camera.png?v=15> Making of: heck the original creator’s other recent posts — BTS footage usually goes up around the same time as the final version.
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/right_arrow.png?v=15> Continuations: Look at the same creator’s profile for follow-up posts (often labeled “part 2,” “update,” “the result,” etc.). Multi-part reels also work — just trim them into two segments.


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/writing_hand.png?v=15> Write the user prompt


Describe the desired output and how it’s different from the input. Include text/label content, position, style, and timestamps when they apply.

	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/white_check_mark.png?v=15> Good example:
	"Generate a video where @bob reacts to this — he should crack up at the punchline around 0:04,
	and add ‘Mood: feral’ as a yellow caption at the bottom from 0:02 to 0:06"

	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/x.png?v=15> Bad example:
	“Make a reaction”


Hard Requirements


*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/camera.png?v=15> Instagram only: every video must come from Instagram. Paste a permalink to a reel or
	video post.
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/stopwatch.png?v=15> Each clip must be at least 4 seconds after trimming.
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/stopwatch.png?v=15> Total video time (all inputs + output combined, after trimming) must be 16 seconds or less.
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/one.png?v=15> The final assistant turn must have exactly ONE video — the related response.
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/link.png?v=15> The output must be a real, related response to the input. Not just a random clip from the same genre or topic.
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/scissors.png?v=15> Two trims from the same post are okay if they capture different moments (like “how it started → how it’s going” from one reel).
*	 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/writing_hand.png?v=15> The user request must be at least 20 words and describe the change — what’s in the output and how it connects to the input (not just describing the input itself). Mention text/labels and timestamps when they’re relevant.


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/star.png?v=15> Note for Quality


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/trophy.png?v=15> One great pair where the output genuinely responds to the input is worth ten generic pairs.

If you find yourself struggling to explain why the output is “related,” it probably isn’t a strong match. Drop it and find a better one!

Subject: Meet Your Fall 2026 Study Away Peers: Join the Virtual Mixer
Body:
Dear Duke Fall Study Away Students, 

 

Curious who else from Duke will be on your study away program this fall? GEO’s Virtual Mixer is a simple way to connect with other students heading to the same program before the semester begins. 

 

You can join the conversation through Duke Groups by following the steps below: 

1.	Join the Global Education Office (GEO) group on Duke Groups: https://duke.campusgroups.com/GEO/club_signup <https://duke.campusgroups.com/GEO/club_signup>  
	(You’ll be prompted to log in with your NetID.) 

2.	Once you’re on the GEO Duke Groups homepage, navigate to the Forum tab. 

3.	Select the thread titled “Fall 2026 Study Away Mixer.” 

4.	Inside the forum, locate the sub-thread for your program and click on it. 
	Tip: Use the “Category” dropdown in the top search bar to sort programs by region. 

5.	To introduce yourself or start a conversation, click your program name and then select the “Comments” button. 

6.	Type your message and click Post. 
	 

The forum is a great place to introduce yourself, find classmates on your program, or start a group chat before departure. Please note that all members of the GEO Duke Groups page can see posts in the forum—even if they are not attending your specific program. For privacy, we recommend avoiding personal contact information in posts. Instead, you might write something like: “Let’s start a program group chat! Reply if you’d like to join!” and then follow up through the Duke Directory. 
 

The Fall 2026 Virtual Study Away Mixer forum is monitored by GEO staff. Please post respectfully; content that violates the Duke Community Standard may be reported to the Office of Student Conduct. 
 

We hope this space helps you start building connections before your study away experience begins. 

 

Happy mixing! 

 
GEO

Hi there,

In this week’s episode of The Coffee Chat Podcast, Ben sits down with Hadley (University of Illinois ’28) to break down the mindset and strategy that helped her secure an Investment Banking Summer Analyst role at BMO. 

They cover: 

*	How to approach recruiting before you feel “ready” 

*	Building technical skills 

*	Structuring effective networking (5–6 coffee chats per week) 

*	Using mock interviews and AI tools to prepare

If memory gives an agent continuity, and action gives it leverage over the world, self-evolution gives it a path to becoming something more than a static system. 

This is the next frontier in agentic AI. The question is no longer just whether an agent can reason, plan, use tools, or execute tasks. It is whether it can improve the way it does those things without waiting for human engineers to redesign it from scratch. 

That shift matters more than it may first appear. Much of machine learning has followed the same broad arc. Early systems depended heavily on handcrafted features, manually chosen pipelines, and human-designed heuristics. Over time, those brittle, labor-intensive components were replaced by learned representations and more automated search procedures. Neural networks displaced hand-engineered features. Neural architecture search began to reduce the need for manually specified network design. AutoML extended this logic further, automating parts of the modeling pipeline that had once required expert intervention. 

Agentic systems are now approaching a similar threshold. 

Today’s agents still depend heavily on manual design. Their prompts are tuned by hand. Their workflows are drafted by researchers. Their tools are selected, composed, and tested through human effort. Their reasoning strategies, evaluation loops, and optimization procedures are often carefully engineered in advance. Yet the stated ambition of the field is to automate more and more of what humans currently do. There is an obvious tension here: systems designed to reduce human labor are themselves still highly dependent on human labor for their construction and improvement. 

That tension will not hold forever. 

The deeper logic of the field points toward self-evolving agents: systems that can refine prompts, redesign workflows, create or improve tools, and eventually optimize entire agent architectures through their own interactions with tasks and environments. In that sense, the destination is not merely better agents. It is agents that can help build better agents. 

This is the architecture of autonomous improvement. 

In what follows, this article examines the major dimensions of self-optimization in intelligent agents. It begins with the broad logic of agent optimization and then moves through four increasingly expansive layers: prompt optimization, workflow optimization, tool optimization, and holistic system-level optimization. Together, these form the emerging machinery of agent self-evolution. 

  	
From Manual Design to Self-Evolving Systems

There is a recurring pattern in the history of AI: what begins as handcrafted engineering often becomes a target for automation. 

That pattern is especially clear in traditional machine learning. Feature design was once a specialist craft. Researchers carefully selected variables, designed representations, and tuned pipelines by hand. Deep learning changed that by shifting representation learning into the model itself. Then even the design of the model began to move toward automation through techniques such as neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimization. AutoML pushed further, reducing the amount of manual intervention required to select models, configure training strategies, and optimize full machine learning pipelines. 

Agentic systems now sit in a similar position to machine learning just before that transition. 

Most current agents are still assembled, not truly grown. Researchers decide what the system prompt should say. They decide how many steps the workflow should contain, which tools should be available, how task decomposition should happen, and what kinds of feedback loops should be used. Even in cases where agents appear autonomous at runtime, their design-time evolution is still largely human-led. 

Yet if the aim is autonomous intelligence, that arrangement looks temporary. 

A mature agentic system should not merely perform tasks. It should improve the way it performs them. It should be able to examine its own failures, revise its strategies, change how it structures subproblems, reconfigure its tool use, and adjust its internal operating procedures in response to new environments or requirements. That is what self-evolution means in practice: not mystical self-awareness, but systematic, iterative self-improvement across the components that determine agent performance. 

This has three immediate attractions. 

The first is scalability. It is expensive to keep improving agents solely by upgrading the underlying foundation model. Retraining or replacing frontier models requires enormous capital, data, and compute. Self-evolution offers another route. An agent may improve substantially by changing its prompts, restructuring its workflow, choosing tools more intelligently, or redesigning task strategies, even if the underlying model remains unchanged. That does not eliminate the importance of stronger base models. But it does provide a cheaper and more flexible way to extract better behavior from existing ones. 

The second is labor reduction. Building agents by hand is still cumbersome. It requires technical expertise, repeated experimentation, and substantial debugging effort. Self-improving systems promise to automate part of that process, lowering the cost of development and making agentic systems more adaptive in the field. 

The third is conceptual alignment with natural intelligence. Humans improve through experience. They refine habits, develop heuristics, learn which tools work best in which situations, and reorganize behavior over time. If artificial agents are meant to become more autonomous, some version of this adaptive loop is not optional. It is essential. 

The result is an emerging research program: to make agent optimization itself a first-class object of design. 

  	
The Optimization Landscape of Intelligent Agents

To understand self-evolution, it helps to think of an agent not as a monolithic entity but as a layered system with multiple optimization surfaces. 

At the base lies prompt optimization. This governs how the agent interacts with the underlying language model: how it frames instructions, requests reasoning, structures constraints, and elicits behavior. 

Above that sits workflow optimization. This concerns how multiple steps, modules, or model invocations are organized into a functioning process. A single prompt may matter, but so does the larger logic of coordination: what happens first, what branches, what loops, what gets checked, and what gets revised. 

Then comes tool optimization. Agents increasingly rely on external tools such as search, APIs, databases, calculators, code interpreters, simulators, and specialized software. Optimizing how those tools are selected, invoked, composed, or even created becomes central to agent performance. 

At the broadest level sits holistic agent optimization. This is the system-wide problem. It treats prompts, workflows, tools, and supporting policies as interacting parts of one evolving architecture. 

These layers are not independent. A better prompt may improve tool use. A different workflow may reduce cost or latency. A new tool may change what workflow structure is best. Holistic optimization matters precisely because local improvements do not always add up to global gains. 

This introduces a familiar problem from machine learning and systems design: multi-objective optimization. Agent performance is not measured along a single axis. Typically, there are at least three competing criteria. 

One is performance in the narrow sense: did the agent solve the task correctly or effectively? 

Another is inference cost: how many model calls, tokens, tools, or compute resources were required? 

The third is latency: how quickly did the system produce a useful result? 

These goals often conflict. A larger workflow with more checking may improve accuracy but increase cost and delay. A faster agent may become shallower or less reliable. A tool-rich system may handle harder tasks but at the cost of orchestration overhead. 

Self-evolution in agents therefore is not just about improving performance in the abstract. It is about learning to navigate these trade-offs intelligently. 

  	
Prompt Optimization: The First Layer of Self-Improvement

Prompt optimization is the most immediate and perhaps most intuitive form of agent self-improvement. 

If the foundation model is the cognitive engine, the prompt is one of the most important ways of steering that engine. Small changes in wording, decomposition strategy, examples, formatting, or constraints can produce large differences in reliability, reasoning quality, or cost. In practice, prompt design often determines whether an agent behaves like a brittle script or a robust problem solver. 

The formal objective is simple: for a task distribution, find the prompt that maximizes expected performance. But the path to that objective is more complicated, because prompt optimization depends on how prompts are evaluated, what signals are produced by that evaluation, and how those signals are used to generate improved prompts. 

How prompts are evaluated

The first issue is evaluation source. In some cases, prompts are assessed against ground truth: a known correct answer, a labeled task outcome, or a benchmark metric. In other cases, only model outputs are available and must be compared against expectations, rules, or alternative outputs. Some systems use pairwise comparison rather than absolute scoring, treating prompt improvement as a relative rather than binary question. 

The second issue is evaluation method. 

Benchmark-based evaluation is the most straightforward. It uses predefined metrics such as accuracy, pass rates, F1, or domain-specific scoring rules. This is scalable and automated, but it only works well when the benchmark captures what really matters. 

A second route is LLM-as-a-judge. Here another language model evaluates the output, often with structured instructions and qualitative criteria. This is especially useful for open-ended tasks where rigid metrics are inadequate. It also allows for richer feedback, including explanations of why an output failed or where a prompt could be improved. 

A third route is human feedback. This remains the most direct way to align prompts with human preferences, especially in ambiguous or creative tasks. But it is costly, slow, and difficult to scale. 

What kinds of feedback matter

Evaluation can generate different forms of signals. 

Numerical signals are simple scores. These are useful for ranking prompts or for optimization loops that depend on scalar objectives. They are easy to automate, but often too coarse to explain why a prompt succeeded or failed. 

Textual signals are more sophisticated. They provide explanations, critiques, and suggested revisions. These are especially powerful when the agent is expected to learn from failure rather than merely detect it. 

Ranking signals occupy the middle ground. Rather than assigning absolute quality, they indicate that one prompt performed better than another. This is often enough to drive improvement without requiring perfect scoring rules. 

How prompts are improved

Once signals exist, optimization can proceed in two broad ways. 

The first is optimization through evaluation signals alone. In effect, the system searches the space of candidate prompts, keeps what works, mutates or recombines it, and repeats. This resembles evolutionary search. It does not require explicit understanding of why a prompt is better, only a reliable way to compare candidates. 

The second is optimization through richer optimization signals. Here the system uses critiques, error analyses, or “textual gradients” to revise prompts more deliberately. Rather than blindly searching, it tries to learn from specific weaknesses: unclear instructions, missing constraints, insufficient decomposition, or poor output formatting. 

This distinction matters because it reflects two different theories of self-improvement. One treats optimization as search. The other treats optimization as reflection. 

In practice, the strongest systems increasingly combine both. 

Why prompt optimization matters

Prompt optimization may sound narrow, but it has broader implications. 

It is often the fastest way to improve agent performance without retraining the base model. It can reduce hallucinations, improve reliability, sharpen tool use, and lower token cost by eliminating wasteful reasoning patterns. It also serves as a prototype for other forms of self-evolution: evaluate, critique, revise, and re-evaluate. 

In that sense, prompt optimization is not merely a practical trick. It is the simplest working example of agents learning to improve themselves. 

  	
Workflow Optimization: Improving the Structure of Thought and Action

If prompt optimization improves how an agent asks a model to think, workflow optimization improves how the system organizes thinking overall. 

This matters because many serious tasks can no longer be solved effectively through a single prompt-response exchange. They require decomposition, intermediate verification, branching strategies, multi-step planning, or coordination across several model invocations. In these settings, the workflow becomes as important as the prompt itself. 

An agentic workflow can be thought of as a structured network of LLM-invoking nodes connected by edges. Each node performs a local function: generate a plan, evaluate evidence, produce a draft, verify a claim, call a tool, critique a result. The edges determine how information moves between those nodes. 

Optimizing the edges

The representation of workflow structure matters. 

A graph-based workflow allows branching, hierarchy, and parallelism. It is useful when tasks require explicit orchestration among specialized steps or subagents. 

A neural-network-like representation introduces non-linear and adaptive interactions. This is less interpretable but can be powerful for learning complex coordination patterns. 

A code-based representation is the most expressive. It supports branching, loops, conditionals, reusable modules, and precise execution logic. It also aligns naturally with language models’ growing competence at generating and modifying code. 

The optimization problem here is not trivial. Changing workflow structure changes the search space itself. A prompt can be revised locally; a workflow redesign may change the agent’s entire operating procedure. 

This has led to a shift from fixed workflows toward generated workflows. Some systems now use language models to produce workflow code or topology directly, then test and revise those workflows based on performance. Others use reinforcement learning or search to optimize the arrangement of nodes and paths. 

The important point is that the workflow is increasingly treated as something dynamic rather than predetermined. 

Optimizing the nodes

Each node in a workflow introduces its own optimization problem. 

Which model should be used? What prompt should it receive? What temperature or decoding parameters are appropriate? What output format should it produce? Should its output be free-form, JSON, XML, executable code, or something else? 

These choices multiply quickly as workflows grow. A multi-node system can become combinatorially difficult to optimize. Yet this node-level tuning matters. The wrong model in the wrong step, or the wrong output format for a downstream tool, can break the entire system. 

This is why workflow optimization is best seen as both structural and parametric. It is not just about drawing a better graph. It is about calibrating each part of that graph to work well within the whole. 

Why workflow optimization matters

A prompt can improve an answer. A workflow can improve a system. 

This is the level at which agents begin to resemble organizations rather than single models. They route work, assign subtasks, create checking procedures, and develop internal division of labor. The quality of those internal arrangements often determines whether agents remain clever demos or become dependable systems. 

Workflow optimization is therefore one of the clearest signs that the field is moving from model use to system design. 

  	
Tool Optimization: Learning to Use and Create Capabilities Beyond the Model

If workflows define how an agent organizes cognition, tools define how it extends cognition into the world. 

Tool use is one of the most consequential developments in agentic AI because it breaks the boundary of the static model. Search lets the agent access current information. Code execution lets it compute. APIs let it interact with services. Databases let it retrieve structured knowledge. Simulators let it test plans. Robotic interfaces let it act physically. 

This makes tool optimization central to self-evolution. 

Learning to use tools

Tool learning can proceed in two main ways. 

The first is learning from demonstrations. Here the agent is shown examples of correct tool use: which tool to call, with what parameters, in what order, and for what purpose. Supervised training or imitation learning can then teach the agent to reproduce those patterns. 

The second is learning from feedback. In this mode, the agent discovers better tool behavior through reward, evaluation, or outcome-based signals. It may learn whether it should have called a tool at all, whether it chose the right one, whether the sequence of calls was efficient, and whether the final outcome justified the cost. 

This second route has become especially important as reinforcement learning methods have improved. Rather than merely predicting tool calls from data, agents can now optimize them based on environmental success. 

The key problems in tool use

Tool optimization is not one problem but several. 

The first is invocation: should the agent use a tool or rely on internal reasoning? Overuse creates cost and latency. Underuse creates errors and hallucinations. 

The second is selection: if a tool is needed, which one should be chosen from the available candidates? 

The third is retrieval efficiency: how fast and accurately can the system identify relevant tools? 

The fourth is planning: for complex tasks, tools often need to be used in sequence, with one result feeding into the next. This makes tool use a planning problem, not just a classification problem. 

The fifth is parameterization and execution fidelity: even if the right tool is selected, poor argument construction or misinterpretation of outputs can derail performance. 

These layers explain why tool optimization matters so much. It is not simply about giving the agent more capabilities. It is about teaching it when, why, and how to use them intelligently. 

Creating new tools

The more ambitious frontier is tool creation. 

Rather than merely using existing tools, some agentic systems are beginning to generate new ones when they identify a capability gap. This usually means writing code, wrapping it into a reusable module, validating it through testing, and then adding it to the agent’s growing toolbox. 

This is a major conceptual shift. It means the agent is no longer limited to a fixed action repertoire. It can expand that repertoire. 

Different approaches emphasize different mechanisms. Some generate tools from examples. Some synthesize utilities from task descriptions. Some create atomic, reusable components that can later be composed into more complex chains. Some use iterative debugging and validation loops to ensure reliability before the tool is incorporated. 

The most interesting implication is cumulative growth. Each solved task can potentially leave behind a new capability. Over time, the agent’s tool library becomes not just an external dependency but a record of its own accumulated problem-solving history. 

That is a powerful form of self-evolution. 

  	
Toward Holistic Agent Optimization

Prompt optimization, workflow optimization, and tool optimization are all important. But optimizing them separately can still leave a system trapped in local optima. 

A better prompt may not help if the workflow is badly structured. A powerful tool may not matter if the prompt never invokes it correctly. A clean workflow may still fail if the model selection or output formatting is misaligned. These interactions are why a broader level of optimization is needed. 

Holistic agent optimization treats the entire agent as a coupled system. 

This approach asks a different question: not how to improve one component, but how to improve the configuration of the whole. That may involve changing prompts, changing workflow topology, changing tools, changing model assignments, or changing the very optimization process itself. 

This is where self-evolution becomes most interesting. 

Some systems now search over entire workflow designs rather than fixed templates. Others evolve codebases that define agent behavior. Some perform self-referential optimization, where the system examines and rewrites parts of its own structure. Others generate new tasks for themselves as a way of expanding capability through self-challenge. 

The unifying idea is that the agent is no longer merely executing a predefined architecture. It is beginning to participate in redesigning that architecture. 

The rise of self-referential systems

This is perhaps the most radical trend in current research. 

A system that can inspect its own prompts and change them is already one kind of self-improver. A system that can rewrite its workflow code, synthesize new tools, generate its own curricula, and create better versions of itself is something more ambitious: a self-referential optimizer. 

That does not mean full autonomy has arrived. These systems remain constrained, brittle, and heavily scaffolded. But the direction is unmistakable. The field is moving from agents that act within systems to agents that modify systems. 

This is the beginning of recursive agency. 

  	
The Real Challenges of Self-Evolution

The idea of self-improving agents is powerful, but it comes with non-trivial challenges. 

One is computational efficiency. Search and optimization across prompts, workflows, tools, and full-system configurations can become extremely expensive. Self-evolution that costs more than manual improvement is not a viable long-term path. 

A second challenge is evaluation. Optimization depends on feedback, and feedback depends on good metrics. For many real-world tasks, success is hard to score cleanly. Overly narrow metrics risk rewarding shallow shortcuts. Poor evaluation creates bad evolution. 

A third challenge is coordination across modules. Improving one component can destabilize another. Holistic optimization is difficult precisely because the system is interdependent. 

A fourth challenge is safety. Agents that can change prompts, workflows, tools, or code raise obvious control questions. Self-evolution without strong constraints can drift into misalignment, unreliability, or unsafe behavior. The same capability that allows autonomous improvement can also produce autonomous failure. 

A fifth challenge is transparency. As systems evolve their own internal procedures, it may become harder for humans to understand why they behave as they do. That creates practical and regulatory problems, especially in high-stakes domains. 

And there is a deeper philosophical issue as well. 

Self-evolution sounds like a purely technical matter, but it is also a governance question. Once improvement becomes endogenous to the system, humans are no longer only designers. They become supervisors of systems that increasingly redesign themselves. 

That is a very different relationship. 

  	
Why This Matters

Self-evolution is not just another feature in the agent stack. It changes the logic of the stack itself. 

A static agent can only be as good as what designers put into it. A self-evolving agent can improve through use, restructure itself around recurring failures, and adapt more efficiently to unfamiliar environments. That makes it potentially more scalable, more resilient, and more autonomous. 

It also brings agentic AI closer to the developmental logic of natural intelligence. Humans do not merely execute. They refine. They revise strategies, discover tools, develop habits, and improve workflows through experience. Artificial agents are now beginning to acquire analogous capabilities, even if in far more primitive and formalized ways. 

The important thing is not that current systems have solved self-improvement. They clearly have not. 

It is that self-improvement has become an explicit design objective. 

That marks a turning point. It means the field is no longer satisfied with making agents that work. It is trying to make agents that become better at working. 

  	
What Comes Next in This Series

This article has focused on how intelligent agents begin to improve themselves. 

That is a decisive step in the broader architecture of autonomy. Once agents can optimize prompts, refine workflows, learn or create tools, and reorganize their own operating procedures, they stop being merely task executors. They become systems capable of directed adaptation. 

But self-evolution introduces another question that is even larger. 

How do these agents behave when they are no longer improving in isolation? 

The next article turns to that problem. It examines how intelligent agents interact with one another in larger systems—how they coordinate, compete, communicate, divide labor, and generate collective behavior across networks rather than single architectures. 

If this article is about how agents improve themselves, the next is about what happens when many such agents begin to evolve and act together. 

That is where the story moves from individual intelligence to collective intelligence—and where agentic systems start to look less like tools and more like ecosystems. 

  	
Series Note: Derived from Advances and Challenges in Foundation Agents

This series draws heavily from the paper Advances and Challenges in Foundation Agents: From Brain-Inspired Intelligence to Evolutionary, Collaborative, and Safe Systems (Aug 2, 2025). The work brings together an impressive group of researchers from institutions including MetaGPT, Mila, Stanford, Microsoft Research, Google DeepMind, and many others to explore the evolving landscape of foundation agents and the challenges that lie ahead. We would like to sincerely thank the authors and researchers who contributed to this outstanding work for compiling such a comprehensive and insightful resource. Their research provides an important foundation for many of the ideas explored throughout this series.

EXERCISE

What Chapter Am I Closing? (A May Reflection for Graduates and Career Transitioners)

 <https://d11n7da8rpqbjy.cloudfront.net/profellow/3831251404827387489_m.jpg> 	
May is graduation season—a time when thousands of people are closing one chapter and beginning another. But transitions aren't just for new graduates walking across a stage in a cap and gown.
 

Maybe you're finishing a degree. Maybe you're leaving a job. Maybe you've been in the same role for years and you're ready for something different. Maybe you just got rejected from an opportunity you wanted and now you're being forced into a transition you didn't choose.
 

Before you rush into the next thing, take time to reflect on what you're actually closing and what you want to begin.
 

JOURNAL EXERCISE:
 

Pull out your journal and reflect on these questions:
 

Part 1: What Chapter Am I Closing?

 

*	What role, identity, or phase of life am I leaving behind right now? (Be specific—"college student," "marketing associate," "person who's been trying to break into consulting for 3 years," etc.)

*	What did this chapter teach me? What skills, relationships, or insights am I taking with me?

*	What am I ready to leave behind from this chapter? (Toxic work culture? Trying to impress people who don't matter? Saying yes to everything? A field that doesn't align with my mission?)

*	What will I miss about this chapter, even if I'm ready to move on?

	 

Part 2: What Chapter Am I Beginning?

 

*	What do I want my next chapter to be about? (Not just a job title—what do I want to be learning, building, or contributing?)

*	What does success look like in this next chapter? 

*	What scares me most about this transition? (Be honest—fear of failure, financial instability, starting over, being behind peers, making the wrong choice?)

*	If I trusted myself completely, what would my next bold move be?

	 

Part 3: How Do I Navigate the In-Between?

 

*	While I'm in transition, what do I need to protect? (My mental health? My financial stability? Time to think strategically rather than react?)

*	What story am I telling myself about this transition—and is it helping or hurting me? ("I'm behind" vs. "I'm being strategic." "I failed" vs. "I'm pivoting.")

*	What's one action I can take this week to move toward my next chapter, even if I don't have all the answers yet?

 

Transitions are hard, but they're also where the most important decisions get made. Don't rush through this moment. Use it strategically.

Subject: Congratulations - You're accepted to the AI Ethics Virtual Exchange
Body:
Dear Graham,

Congratulations! You have been accepted to the AI Ethics Virtual Exchange <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fopenhandsinitiative.org%2Fprograms%2Fvirtual.html&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7Cabca1e29ca1a40de815c08deb038dd60%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639141956506714378%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C60000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=J0nVYsMWhjoaurxZFOZDOAwYwqv4tlLNtcqmZadSH5g%3D&reserved=0> , part of the Coffee & Conversation program hosted by the Open Hands Initiative. 

We received applications from people in more than 30 countries with a wide diversity of backgrounds. Accepted fellows bring experience from the business sector, academia, science, technology, health care, politics, and more. We cannot wait have you share your knowledge with your global peers.

*** To secure your spot in the program, please sign our Waiver and Code of Conduct, which will be sent separately via email from JotForm. We do this to ensure a space that is safe for respectful and meaningful dialogue. If you have any questions or concerns about it, please let us know.***

Once you have signed the waiver, you will receive a link to the Google Classroom, along with a detailed copy of the syllabus, and calendar invitations with the Zoom links for each session. 

Welcome aboard! We can’t wait to meet you!

Kind regards,
The Open Hands Initiative Team

Subject: Virtual LBO Model Workshop
Body:
Register for Duke LBO Model Virtual Workshop 

 

Interested in a career in private equity or investment banking? Join us July 13-17 (3:30pm-4:15pm EDT daily) for a virtual workshop to learn how to create a leveraged buyout (LBO) financial model, a key Excel tool used in private equity investing. This workshop is open to all Duke students.  Registrants should have a general understanding of financial accounting and corporate finance and be prepared to complete 1 to 2 hours of self-paced homework outside of each virtual session.  Video guides will be provided for each assignment, and all live sessions will be recorded.  Therefore, it is not essential to attend all sessions, but students who know they can’t attend any of the sessions should not sign up for this workshop.

 

Registration link  <https://signup.fuqua.duke.edu/nextevent/modernevent/lboworkshop2026>  ($200 registration fee, $50 early bird discount if you register by May 29)

 

Full Workshop Description <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Uu9cWT9vp6uAUuBfIa0guB0gIgHADwMpXfZMjCJBg9c/edit?usp=sharing>

History repeats


President Trump said yesterday that U.S. negotiations with Tehran were on “life support.” Why? Among other things, Iran wants to maintain control of the Strait of Hormuz.

A fifth of the world’s oil supply flowed through that passage before the war, and now Iran has choked it off. Iranian attacks on passing vessels and a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports have trapped thousands of ships in the Persian Gulf, inducing a global economic crisis. The crisis looms over Trump’s summit with China’s president, Xi Jinping, later this week. Trump wants Xi to lean on Iran to reopen the strait.

This keeps happening.

Iran and Iraq stopped ships in the Persian Gulf during the war between those two countries in the 1980s. The conflict spread. Iranian forces intercepted ships bound for Iraq and its allies. It led to a small if deadly naval war that killed more than 400 civilian sailors and damaged 500 commercial vessels along with American warships.

Iran’s ability to control the strait is a recurring headache for U.S. military leaders. “If you ask me what keeps me awake at night, it’s the Strait of Hormuz,” one commander said in 2012. Fighting there, another said, “would be like a knife fight in a phone booth.”


Who owns the water?


Scholars have argued for centuries that no state can lay claim to the high seas, the ocean common. One jurist from the Dutch Golden Age came up with a term for it: mare liberum, or free sea.

Which is fine out in the middle of an ocean. It gets a little more complicated closer to shore, and particularly with choke points like the Strait of Hormuz. For decades, the United States has argued that it has a right to freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran, in contrast, has said that it can regulate traffic there.

By what right? Can a nation declare the waters off its coastline as its own? How far out do those waters extend?

I picked up some light reading: “Legal Vortex in the Strait of Hormuz,” a 2014 paper by James Kraska, a professor at the U.S. Naval War College. It could have been written much more recently — like, in February. We spoke yesterday. Kraska has seen this conflict coming for more than a decade.

What’s going on in the strait is fundamentally a legal dispute, he told me. The U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, a kind of international constitution for the oceans, governs passage there. Neither Washington nor Tehran has ratified it, but it reflects “customary international law,” which means it is still supposed to be binding, Kraska told me.

In other words, Iran can claim that its territorial waters extend 12 nautical miles from its shoreline, which is permitted by the treaty, but only if it recognizes the right of free navigation through those waters. (Free navigation, Kraska noted. Charging a toll, as Iran hopes to do, would break the law.)

Kraska told me about a similar conflict between Britain and Albania in the late 1940s, over the channel between Greece and the island of Corfu. In an effort to control that strait, Albania fired on Royal Navy warships. Mines in the strait killed dozens of sailors. It didn’t lead to war. The case became the first one adjudicated by the International Court of Justice. It ruled that Britain enjoyed the right to sail through and that Albania had a duty to keep the strait clear of mines.

Albania, a less powerful nation than Iran, complied. The precedent may end there.

A Securities and Exchange Commission proposal <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45669000.234450%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuc2VjLmdvdi9uZXdzcm9vbS9wcmVzcy1yZWxlYXNlcy8yMDI2LTQyLXNlYy1wcm9wb3Nlcy1hbWVuZG1lbnRzLXBlcm1pdC1vcHRpb25hbC1zZW1pYW5udWFsLXJlcG9ydGluZy1wdWJsaWMtY29tcGFuaWVzP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBa60e97b3&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C58e0419d9a0742623a3c08deb0131e02%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639141793332230937%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=3t5YVH5du7fMuiuHX2h227JccG5uP%2BZ3yAXX7l9GJMs%3D&reserved=0>  that would allow companies to skip quarterly financial reports <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45669000.234450%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9maW5hbmNlL3JlZ3VsYXRpb24vc2VjLXByb3Bvc2VzLXRvLWVsaW1pbmF0ZS1xdWFydGVybHktcmVwb3J0aW5nLXJlcXVpcmVtZW50LWZvci1wdWJsaWMtY29tcGFuaWVzLTNjMGM5ZmRjP21vZD1kamVtTWFya2V0c0FN%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dBb8e6a0f1&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C58e0419d9a0742623a3c08deb0131e02%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639141793332289597%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=zqiCgVpZZc6Q8XpQyn6cdaJ7pFgZJXcvGt7XozoUwDg%3D&reserved=0> , opting for twice-a-year instead, might be another misstep. One stated goal is to encourage more companies to list on public exchanges.

 

The measure, championed last year by President Trump <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45669000.234450%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9maW5hbmNlL3JlZ3VsYXRpb24vdHJ1bXAtY2FsbHMtZm9yLWVuZGluZy1xdWFydGVybHktZWFybmluZ3MtcmVwb3J0cy03MWUzYWZhYT9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB0dc4ad75&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C58e0419d9a0742623a3c08deb0131e02%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639141793332361797%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=Q6m3%2B4Nok7R3nt%2BnSdrBK1uOnqf%2Fjn1u2jW4mARcc2I%3D&reserved=0> , would be voluntary and might save some companies a bit up front. But the SEC should study Britain’s disappointing experience after a similar change.

 

The U.K. government cited corporate short-termism, not costs, when it scrapped quarterly reporting requirements in 2014. Research by Shivaram Rajgopal, a professor of accounting and auditing at Columbia Business School, shows zero change in things like research and development spending. 

 

Meanwhile, investors have less information. He isn’t a fan of the SEC proposal either.

 

“This is a solution looking for a problem,” says Rajgopal.

 

At first, relatively few British companies stopped reporting quarterly. It’s also unlikely that big, widely held U.S. companies would be in a rush. Investors might initially assume “something is wrong with you,” says Rajgopal. 

 

But a decade after the requirement was dropped in the U.K., less-frequent reporting has become the norm. Analyst coverage has fallen meaningfully too, says Rajgopal. There’s less to analyze.

 

Of all times to propose the change in the U.S., now is an odd one. Some of the biggest initial public offerings ever are looming. Investors and analysts are still getting to know companies after their IPOs, so quarterly updates are watched extra carefully. 

 

It’s also odd because lower accounting and audit requirements for certain U.S. IPOs have enabled a rash of scams recently <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrk.wsj.com%2Fclick%2F45669000.234450%2FaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cud3NqLmNvbS9maW5hbmNlL3N0b2Nrcy9ob3ctYS1wdXNoLWZvci1tb3JlLWlwb3MtZnVlbGVkLWEtd2F2ZS1vZi1zY2Ftcy1mNjYwM2IxOT9tb2Q9ZGplbU1hcmtldHNBTQ%2F6965299853e1c001a97cb68dB846dc787&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C58e0419d9a0742623a3c08deb0131e02%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639141793332422531%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=qv14txxMN75hrUVZTcIfUdsajSKJfwDuWqHsdxaQaQk%3D&reserved=0> . Those “emerging growth companies,” listed through the 2012 JOBS Act, were typically foreign-domiciled and traded on the Nasdaq.

 

There’s clearly room for improvement. Securities filings are packed with repetitive legalese few will read, while the juicy bits in the footnotes require some expertise to understand. 

 

Meanwhile, financial press releases for mass consumption are filled with creative interpretations of profitability such as “adjusted Ebitda.” The only requirement is that the difference with generally accepted accounting principles be explained somewhere.

 

Making transparency less about box-ticking and more about truly informing investors would be a real step forward.

Reporter Micah Maidenberg explains how Amazon and a host of other companies are trying to catch up with SpaceX’s Starlink network:

A: Low-Earth orbit is often defined as between around 100 miles and 1,200 miles above ground. It’s home to well-known spacecraft such as the International Space Station and the Hubble Space Telescope.

For internet satellite operators, LEO has some real advantages: Satellites closer to Earth usually offer better performance to users on the ground than those stationed further out in space.

Thousands of these satellites are expected to be launched in the years ahead by SpaceX, Amazon.com, Blue Origin and Chinese satellite operators, among others. Internet satellites, wherever they’re located in space, are part of the lucrative market for high-speed internet connections.

	“I see now that most of the choices I agonized over, shed tears over, lost sleep over, had a perfectly accessible ‘un-do’ button. I treated every fork in the road like it was permanent, and almost none of them were. Hi team!  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/smile.png?v=15> 

We want to share important feedback we just received today for the following project.

*	vs-1778016225-ig-entity-tagging-v1

Please make sure to follow the guidelines and take this feedback into account, you will find that achieving good scores becomes much easier  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/raising_hands.png?v=15>  <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/down_arrow.png?v=15> 

________________________________


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/x.png?v=15> Common Errors


*	Reference image issues: The reference images do not contain the entity that was tagged.
*	Missing tagging / incomplete coverage: Primary and / or secondary items have been left untagged.
*	Wrong entity types: Wrong selection of clothing/ product/ style, e.g. eyeglasses have been tagged as products, not clothing.
*	Bounding box + spatial precision: bounding boxes are too big or too small, not tight enough around the object, or cropped strangely.
*	Info/logo/ brand tagging issues: missing logos, information tags, and/ or brand labeling.


 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/white_check_mark.png?v=15> Recommendations


*	Ensure that the reference image contains exactly the entity that has been tagged, not just something that looks similar.
*	Ensure that all of the entities have been tagged (every person, every clothing item, every product, every place, every animal, every visible logo or sign)
*	Label each entity accurately and double-check the Entity Types when in doubt: eyeglasses fall under clothing, not products.
*	Ensure all bounding boxes are precise.
*	Ensure that all necessary info, logo or brand entities have been accurately tagged.

 <https://emoji.discourse-cdn.com/twitter/x.png?v=15> Common Errors


*	Incorrect scene segmentation: a frequent issue is the unnecessary division of scenes when the setting or location remains the same.

	*	The auditors have noted that multiple scenes were often created for a single location or when only minor visual changes (like photo transitions) occurred.

*	Missing or incomplete atomic actions: auditors have been seeing quite a few tasks in which the distinct actions within the videos were not captured or segmented, leading to gaps in the annotation.

*	Labeling inconsistencies and lack of detail: auditors have been identifying tasks with labeling inconsistencies, incorrect details, or lack of specificity in scene and action labels.

	*	For example: misgendering subjects, not including locations alongside the verb and object, etc.

*	Technical timing and camera movement errors: missing scene cuts in single shot videos, small gaps between segments, and incorrect camera movement labels.

The Persian Gulf countries are struggling to export their oil because Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz. Why don’t they just build an oil pipeline across Saudi Arabia? | Will Karlin, Denver, Colorado

Vivian Nereim, the Gulf bureau chief, writes:

Saudi Arabia actually did build an oil pipeline to bypass the strait, decades ago, to prepare for a moment like this. It was transporting up to seven million barrels per day of oil — until it was bombed during the Iran war, reducing its capacity by around 10 percent. The vulnerability of pipelines is one reason that this one isn’t a cure-all. Another is that the six Gulf countries are economic competitors that often have tense political relationships; the Gulf countries are not always inclined to share. So a cross-border project would be a tall order.

Are manufacturing jobs coming back, as Donald Trump said they would when he ran for office? | Amy Richards, Mission, Kansas

Alan Rappeport, who covers economic policy, writes:

On “Liberation Day” a year ago, President Trump said that his sweeping global tariffs would bring jobs and factories “roaring back” to the United States. But manufacturing employment continues to decline, and more than 80,000 of those jobs have been lost since he took office. That’s because the tariffs impose additional costs on domestic producers that rely on imports to make their goods, so it’s harder for them to expand and hire. The administration also noted this month that manufacturing wages and labor productivity are both rising — tech advances mean factories need fewer people to do the same work. Both things make it harder to hire.

✏️ President Trump’s announcement that the U.S. military would blockade the Strait of Hormuz sets off a high-stakes war of attrition <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail19.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gktzkk-hrkusddg-h%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C32a9125e6a0f47a8f39208de9945e254%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116722631501917%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=n3adWjacFZZx2q2IvT6067BaAz9MtOrt%2FV0Crqoxn9o%3D&reserved=0>  that will test who has the higher threshold for pain: Iran or the global markets. The WSJ’s Robbie Gramer and Alex Leary found out from officials close to the president what could be next in the conflict after U.S. peace talks with Iran broke down in Pakistan. Trump remains open to a diplomatic off-ramp, aides said. But for now, the White House is considering a menu of options <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail19.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gktzkk-hrkusddg-k%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C32a9125e6a0f47a8f39208de9945e254%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116722631516484%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=uSSqgkdv9R5zBnbzDl8NUmWrhpfTUZrCdadK1Ix7vV4%3D&reserved=0> —including military strikes—alongside its blockade to break a stalemate. Q: The economy is growing, so why aren't we seeing job growth? 


An unusual divergence between GDP and new jobs shows worker productivity is making up for a slowdown <https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2F10point.cmail19.com%2Ft%2Fd-l-gktzkk-hrkusddg-yd%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cgraham.mills%40duke.edu%7C32a9125e6a0f47a8f39208de9945e254%7Ccb72c54e4a314d9eb14a1ea36dfac94c%7C0%7C0%7C639116722631768147%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=fPD4pwqsjWBUje9WJeFmefXbdDyaav6cu93NcYfbcag%3D&reserved=0>  in immigration and the labor force, explains economics correspondent Harriet Torry.

A: For the past year, two prominent indicators have told opposite stories of the economy’s health: The economy itself grew in 2025, but despite a solid March, jobs didn’t.

This puzzle could have an encouraging explanation: Productivity has revived at just the right time.

There are two main ways to grow the economy. The first is to add workers. This, though, has become harder since Trump’s policies brought most immigration to a halt, while an aging workforce and a decadeslong drop in birth rates have sapped growth in the native-born labor force. That leaves the second channel: Make the workers you have more productive.

According to the Labor Department, output per hour in the nonfarm business sector rose 2.1% last year. Growth has also averaged 2.1% over the past six years, a pickup from the 1.5% a year average from 2007 to 2019.

This comes amid a falloff in labor-force and job growth. In the year through March, the labor force—people working or looking for a job—declined by 554,000.

With fewer entrants, the “breakeven” rate of new jobs needed to keep unemployment stable has fallen. This helps explain why the jobless rate remains low even as job creation flatlined.

Economists say it is too early to determine AI’s exact role, but expect it is helping.

Congratulations on receiving an unconditional offer to the Undergraduate Study Abroad Program (One Semester) in Semester 2, 2026. We're excited to welcome you to our community and campus.

 

Studying at the University of Sydney means you'll be opening the door to countless opportunities and receiving an education at one of the world's top 25 universities*, with over 175 years of experience in achieving excellence and serving the community as Australia's first university.

Back by popular demand, B-Randy House Council will be hosting an East Campus Blood Drive this Friday, April 17th, from 11:00 AM to 4:00 PM at GADU.

Your donation can help save lives while also giving back to a cause that matters.

We encourage all eligible residents to come out, participate, and spread the word. Every donor makes a difference.

Subject: Italian 101 tutoring hour tomorrow practice for oral exam
Body:
Ciao a tutti,

Domani, lunedì 13 dall’1:15-2:15 a Languages 04 pratica per l’esame orale!

Would you like to get some practice before your oral exams on Wednesday and Friday? I would love to help,  I’ll be in my office, Languages 04 tomorrow, Monday, April 13th between 1:15-2:15.  

Go down to the basement in the Languages building, turn right at the bottom of the stairs, open the door, go down the corridor until you find 04.  Please note: this is NOT the group office 014 to the left of the stairs.

A domani,
Laura
